items.title: Operators
explanation: Simple Meaning
Operators are special symbols or keywords used to perform operations on values and variables.
Simple Definition: Operators tell Python what operation to perform on one or more values.
a = 10 b = 5 print(a + b)
Here, + is an operator. It tells Python to add a and b.
a + b ↓ ↓ 10 5 \ / + ↓ 15
Main Types of Python Operators

Operator TypePurpose
ArithmeticPerform mathematical operations
ComparisonCompare two values
LogicalCombine conditions
AssignmentAssign or update values
MembershipCheck whether a value exists in a collection
IdentityCheck whether two references point to the same object
Python Operators │ ├── Arithmetic ├── Comparison ├── Logical ├── Assignment ├── Membership └── Identity
1. Arithmetic Operators
Arithmetic operators are used for mathematical calculations.

OperatorOperationExampleResult
+Addition10 + 515
-Subtraction10 - 55
*Multiplication10 * 550
/Division10 / 52.0
//Floor Division10 // 33
%Modulus10 % 31
**Exponent2 ** 38
a = 10 b = 3 print(a + b) print(a - b) print(a * b) print(a / b) print(a // b) print(a % b) print(a ** b)
Floor Division //
Floor division returns the whole-number part of the division result.
print(10 // 3)
Output:
3
10 / 3 = 3.333... 10 // 3 = 3 ↑ Whole-number result
Modulus %
The modulus operator returns the remainder after division.
print(10 % 3)
Output:
1
10 ÷ 3 3 × 3 = 9 10 - 9 = 1 Remainder = 1 ↓ 10 % 3 = 1
Common Use: The modulus operator is useful for checking whether a number is even or odd.
number = 10 if number % 2 == 0: print("Even")
2. Comparison Operators
Comparison operators compare two values and return either True or False.

OperatorMeaningExample
==Equal to10 == 10 → True
!=Not equal to10 != 5 → True
>Greater than10 > 5 → True
<Less than10 < 5 → False
>=Greater than or equal to10 >= 10 → True
<=Less than or equal to5 <= 10 → True
a = 10 b = 5 print(a == b) print(a != b) print(a > b) print(a < b) print(a >= b) print(a <= b)
Important: = assigns a value, while == compares two values.
age = 25 # Assignment print(age == 25) # Comparison
= → Store a value age = 25 == → Compare values age == 25 ↓ True
3. Logical Operators
Logical operators are used to combine or reverse conditions.

OperatorMeaning
andTrue when both conditions are True
orTrue when at least one condition is True
notReverses a boolean value
and Operator
age = 25 has_id = True print(age >= 18 and has_id)
Output:
True
Condition 1: age >= 18 → True Condition 2: has_id → True True AND True ↓ True
or Operator
is_admin = False is_manager = True print(is_admin or is_manager)
Output:
True
False OR True ↓ True Only one condition needs to be True.
not Operator
is_active = True print(not is_active)
Output:
False
not True ↓ False not False ↓ True
Logical Operator Summary

ABA and BA or B
TrueTrueTrueTrue
TrueFalseFalseTrue
FalseTrueFalseTrue
FalseFalseFalseFalse
4. Assignment Operators
Assignment operators are used to assign or update values in variables.

OperatorExampleEquivalent To
=x = 10Assign 10 to x
+=x += 5x = x + 5
-=x -= 5x = x - 5
*=x *= 5x = x * 5
/=x /= 5x = x / 5
//=x //= 5x = x // 5
%=x %= 5x = x % 5
**=x **= 2x = x ** 2
count = 10 count += 5 print(count)
Output:
15
count = 10 count += 5 ↓ count = count + 5 ↓ count = 15
5. Membership Operators
Membership operators check whether a value exists inside a collection such as a string, list, tuple, set, or dictionary.

OperatorMeaning
inReturns True if the value exists
not inReturns True if the value does not exist
languages = ["Python", "SQL", "Java"] print("Python" in languages) print("C++" in languages)
Output:
True False
languages ↓ [Python, SQL, Java] "Python" in languages ↓ True "C++" in languages ↓ False
not in Example
languages = ["Python", "SQL", "Java"] print("C++" not in languages)
Output:
True
Data Engineering Use: Membership operators are useful when checking whether expected columns, values, or records exist in data.
columns = ["id", "name", "salary"] if "salary" in columns: print("Column exists")
6. Identity Operators
Identity operators check whether two variables refer to the same object in memory.

OperatorMeaning
isTrue if both references point to the same object
is notTrue if both references do not point to the same object
a = None print(a is None)
Output:
True
Important: Use == to compare values. Use is when checking object identity. A common example is checking x is None.
x = 10 y = 10 print(x == y)
== checks whether the values are equal.
Data Engineering Example ⭐
Operators are frequently used when processing, validating, and transforming data.

record_count = 100 failed_records = 5 success_records = record_count - failed_records if success_records > 0: print("Data processed") if failed_records == 0: print("No failures") else: print("Some records failed")
Input Data ↓ record_count = 100 failed_records = 5 ↓ Arithmetic Operator 100 - 5 = 95 ↓ Comparison Operator 95 > 0 ↓ True ↓ Processing continues
Common Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Using = instead of == if age = 18: Correct: if age == 18: ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Confusing / and // 10 / 3 → 3.333... 10 // 3 → 3 ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Using is to compare normal values Use == for value comparison. ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Forgetting operator order result = 10 + 5 * 2 ↓ 20, not 30
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
Arithmetic ↓ Calculate Comparison ↓ Compare Logical ↓ Combine conditions Assignment ↓ Store or update Membership ↓ Check existence Identity ↓ Check same object
Quick Summary

TypeMain OperatorsPurpose
Arithmetic+ - * / // % **Calculations
Comparison== != > < >= <=Compare values
Logicaland or notCombine conditions
Assignment= += -= *=Assign/update values
Membershipin not inCheck existence
Identityis is notCheck object identity
Final Definition: Python operators are symbols or keywords used to perform calculations, compare values, combine conditions, assign values, check membership, and check object identity.

Step 7: Build a small data validation example.

items.title: Truthy and Falsy Values
explanation: Simple Meaning
In Python, every value can be treated as either True or False when Python evaluates it in a condition.
Simple Definition: A truthy value behaves like True, while a falsy value behaves like False in a condition.
value = "Python" if value: print("Value exists")
Since the string "Python" is non-empty, Python treats it as True.
value = "Python" ↓ Non-empty string ↓ Truthy ↓ Condition is treated as True
What Does Truthy Mean?
A truthy value is not necessarily equal to the Boolean value True. It simply behaves as True when Python checks it in a Boolean context.
print(bool("Python")) print(bool(100)) print(bool([1, 2, 3]))
Output:
True True True
What Does Falsy Mean?
A falsy value behaves as False when Python evaluates it in a Boolean context.
print(bool(0)) print(bool("")) print(bool([]))
Output:
False False False
Common Falsy Values
The following commonly used values are treated as falsy in Python.

ValueTypeBoolean Result
FalseboolFalse
NoneNoneTypeFalse
0intFalse
0.0floatFalse
""Empty stringFalse
[]Empty listFalse
{}Empty dictionaryFalse
()Empty tupleFalse
set()Empty setFalse
Common Falsy Values │ ├── False ├── None ├── 0 ├── 0.0 ├── "" ├── [] ├── {} ├── () └── set()
Common Truthy Values
Generally, non-empty collections, non-empty strings, and non-zero numbers are truthy.

ValueWhy?Boolean Result
TrueBoolean TrueTrue
1Non-zero numberTrue
-10Non-zero numberTrue
"Python"Non-empty stringTrue
[1, 2]Non-empty listTrue
{"name": "Nani"}Non-empty dictionaryTrue
(1, 2)Non-empty tupleTrue
{1, 2}Non-empty setTrue
Easy Rule: Empty values and zero are usually falsy. Non-empty values and non-zero numbers are usually truthy.
Using bool()
The bool() function converts a value into its Boolean representation.
print(bool(1)) print(bool(0)) print(bool("Hello")) print(bool(""))
Output:
True False True False
Value ↓ bool(value) ↓ True or False
Truthy and Falsy in if Statements ⭐
Python automatically checks the truthiness of a value inside an if statement.
name = "Nani" if name: print("Name is available")
Because name contains a non-empty string, the condition is truthy.
name = "" if name: print("Name is available") else: print("Name is empty")
Output:
Name is empty
if value: ↓ Python checks bool(value) ↓ True? → Run if block False? → Skip if block
Checking Lists
You can directly check whether a list contains values.
records = [101, 102, 103] if records: print("Records available")
A non-empty list is truthy.
records = [] if records: print("Records available") else: print("No records found")
Output:
No records found
records = [] ↓ Empty list ↓ Falsy ↓ else block runs
Checking Strings
file_name = "data.csv" if file_name: print("File name available")
A non-empty string is truthy.
file_name = "" if not file_name: print("File name is missing")
The not operator reverses the Boolean result.
file_name = "" ↓ Falsy → False ↓ not False ↓ True ↓ if block runs
Checking None
None represents the absence of a value and is falsy.
result = None if result: print("Result available") else: print("No result available")
Output:
No result available
Important: Although None is falsy, use is None when you specifically want to check whether a value is None.
result = None if result is None: print("No result available")
Truthy/Falsy with Logical Operators
Truthy and falsy values are also important when using and, or, and not.
name = "Nani" age = 25 if name and age: print("Both values are available")
Both values are truthy, so the condition runs.
name = "" age = 25 if name or age: print("At least one value is available")
The condition runs because age is truthy.
Difference Between False and Falsy

ConceptMeaning
FalseThe actual Boolean value False
FalsyAny value that behaves like False in a Boolean context
print(False == 0) print(bool(False)) print(bool(0))
Both False and 0 are falsy, but they are different concepts.
Falsy Values │ ├── False ├── 0 ├── "" ├── [] ├── {} └── None All behave as False in a Boolean context
Data Engineering Example ⭐
Truthy and falsy values are useful when checking whether data is available before processing it.
records = [ {"id": 1, "name": "Nani"}, {"id": 2, "name": "Kumar"} ] if records: print("Starting data processing") else: print("No records to process")
Data Source ↓ records ↓ Check: if records ↓ Non-empty? ── Yes → Process data │ No ↓ No records to process
Checking Missing Data
You may also use truthy and falsy checks when validating simple values.
file_path = "" if not file_path: print("File path is required")
file_path = "" ↓ Falsy ↓ not file_path ↓ True ↓ Show missing value message
Data Engineering Tip: Before processing data, it is common to check whether a collection or input contains values. For example, if records: checks whether the collection is non-empty.
Common Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Assuming only False is falsy Falsy values also include: 0, "", [], {}, (), None ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Checking a list unnecessarily if len(records) > 0: Often simpler: if records: ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Using == None Less preferred: if value == None: Preferred: if value is None: ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Assuming 0 means None 0 is falsy, but it is still a valid number.
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
Truthy ↓ Usually non-empty or non-zero Examples: 1 "Python" [1, 2] {"id": 1} ──────────────── Falsy ↓ Usually empty, zero, False, or None Examples: False None 0 "" [] {} () set()
Quick Summary

ConceptKey Point
TruthyBehaves like True in a Boolean context
FalsyBehaves like False in a Boolean context
bool()Converts a value to True or False
Non-empty stringTruthy
Empty stringFalsy
Non-zero numberTruthy
ZeroFalsy
Non-empty collectionTruthy
Empty collectionFalsy
NoneFalsy

Final Definition: Truthy and falsy values describe how Python treats values in Boolean contexts. Non-empty and non-zero values are generally truthy, while False, None, zero, and empty collections are commonly falsy.
practice: Step 1: Use bool() to check different values.
print(bool(True)) print(bool(False)) print(bool(1)) print(bool(0)) print(bool("Python")) print(bool(""))
Step 2: Check empty and non-empty collections.
print(bool([1, 2, 3])) print(bool([])) print(bool({"name": "Nani"})) print(bool({})) print(bool((1, 2))) print(bool(()))
Step 3: Use a truthy value in an if statement.
name = "Nani" if name: print("Name is available")
Step 4: Check an empty list.
records = [] if records: print("Records available") else: print("No records found")
Step 5: Check a missing string value using not.
file_name = "" if not file_name: print("File name is required")
Step 6: Check whether a value is specifically None.
result = None if result is None: print("Result is None")
Step 7: Create a simple data processing check.
records = [101, 102, 103] if records: print("Processing", len(records), "records") else: print("No records available")
Final Understanding Check:

Is an empty list truthy or falsy? 8. Is None truthy or falsy? 9. What does bool() do? 10. Why can you write if records:? 11. What does not do to a falsy value? 12. What is the preferred way to check whether a value is None?
Practice Goal: You should be able to identify common truthy and falsy values and use them correctly in conditions and simple data validation checks.

items.title: Conditional Statements
explanation: Simple Meaning
Conditional statements allow a Python program to make decisions and execute different code depending on whether a condition is True or False.
Simple Definition: Conditional statements are used to control which block of code runs based on a condition.
age = 18 if age >= 18: print("Eligible")
Since age >= 18 is True, Python executes the if block.
Condition ↓ True or False? ↓ True → Run selected code False → Skip or run another block
Why Do We Need Conditional Statements?
Programs often need to make decisions based on input, data, or a particular situation.
temperature = 35 if temperature > 30: print("Hot day")
The program checks the condition and decides whether the message should be printed.
Key Idea: Conditions help a program choose what to do next.
Types of Conditional Statements
Conditional Statements │ ├── if ├── if...else └── if...elif...else
The if Statement
The if statement runs a block of code only when its condition is True.
if condition: # code to run when condition is True
marks = 80 if marks >= 50: print("Passed")
Output:
Passed
marks >= 50? ↓ True ↓ Print "Passed"
What Happens When the if Condition Is False?
If the condition is False, Python skips the code inside the if block.
marks = 40 if marks >= 50: print("Passed") print("Program finished")
Output:
Program finished
marks >= 50? ↓ False ↓ Skip if block ↓ Continue program
The if...else Statement
Use else when you want one block to run if the condition is True and another block to run if it is False.
if condition: # runs when True else: # runs when False
age = 16 if age >= 18: print("Eligible") else: print("Not eligible")
Output:
Not eligible
age >= 18? ↓ ┌──True──→ Eligible │ False ↓ Not eligible
The elif Statement
elif means else if. It allows you to check another condition when the previous condition is False.
if condition1: # code elif condition2: # code else: # code
marks = 75 if marks >= 90: print("Grade A") elif marks >= 60: print("Grade B") else: print("Grade C")
Output:
Grade B
marks = 75 ↓ marks >= 90? → False ↓ marks >= 60? → True ↓ Print "Grade B" ↓ Remaining blocks are skipped
Order of Conditions Is Important ⭐
Python checks conditions from top to bottom. Once it finds the first condition that is True, it runs that block and skips the remaining elif and else blocks.
marks = 95 if marks >= 60: print("Passed") elif marks >= 90: print("Excellent")
Output:
Passed
The first condition is already true, so Python never checks the elif condition.
A better order is:
marks = 95 if marks >= 90: print("Excellent") elif marks >= 60: print("Passed") else: print("Failed")
Important: Place more specific conditions before broader conditions when their ranges overlap.
Using Comparison Operators in Conditions

OperatorMeaningExample
==Equal toa == b
!=Not equal toa != b
>Greater thana > b
<Less thana < b
>=Greater than or equal toa >= b
<=Less than or equal toa <= b
number = 10 if number == 10: print("Number is 10")
Using Logical Operators
You can combine multiple conditions using logical operators.
age = 25 country = "India" if age >= 18 and country == "India": print("Condition matched")
and
The result is true only when both conditions are true.
if age >= 18 and age <= 60: print("Working age")
or
The result is true when at least one condition is true.
day = "Sunday" if day == "Saturday" or day == "Sunday": print("Weekend")
not
The not operator reverses the Boolean result.
is_active = False if not is_active: print("Account is inactive")
Truthy and Falsy Values in Conditions
Python conditions do not always need comparison operators. Python can directly evaluate whether a value is truthy or falsy.
name = "Nani" if name: print("Name is available")
A non-empty string is truthy, so the if block runs.
records = [] if records: print("Records available") else: print("No records found")
Output:
No records found
Remember: Empty strings, empty collections, 0, False, and None are commonly treated as falsy.
Nested Conditional Statements
A nested conditional statement is an if statement inside another conditional block.
age = 25 has_id = True if age >= 18: if has_id: print("Access allowed") else: print("ID required") else: print("Underage")
age >= 18? ↓ True ↓ has_id? ┌──True──→ Access allowed │ False ↓ ID required
Nested conditions are useful, but avoid making code unnecessarily deep when a simpler condition can be used.
Data Engineering Example ⭐
Conditional statements are commonly used to validate data before processing it.
records = [101, 102, 103] if records: print("Starting data processing") else: print("No records to process")
Data Source ↓ Records received? ↓ ┌──Yes──→ Process records │ No ↓ No records to process
Example: Data Validation
age = None if age is None: print("Age is missing") elif age < 0: print("Invalid age") else: print("Valid age")
Data Engineering Use: Conditions are useful for checking missing values, validating data, handling errors, and deciding how data should be processed.
Common Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Using = instead of == if age = 18: Correct: if age == 18: ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Forgetting the colon if age >= 18 Correct: if age >= 18: ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Incorrect indentation if age >= 18: print("Eligible") Correct: if age >= 18: print("Eligible") ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Incorrect condition order if marks >= 60: print("Passed") elif marks >= 90: print("Excellent") More specific conditions should come first.
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
if ↓ Check one condition if + else ↓ Choose between two paths if + elif + else ↓ Choose between multiple paths Python checks ↓ Top to Bottom ↓ First True condition wins
Quick Summary

ConceptKey Point
ifRuns code when a condition is True
elseRuns when previous conditions are False
elifChecks another condition
Condition orderPython checks from top to bottom
First True conditionIts block runs and remaining blocks are skipped
andBoth conditions must be True
orAt least one condition must be True
notReverses the Boolean result
IndentationDefines the conditional code block

Final Definition: Conditional statements allow a Python program to make decisions by checking conditions and executing different blocks of code depending on whether those conditions evaluate to True or False.
practice: Step 1: Create a simple if statement.
age = 20 if age >= 18: print("Adult")
Step 2: Use if...else.
number = 7 if number % 2 == 0: print("Even") else: print("Odd")
Step 3: Use if...elif...else.
marks = 75 if marks >= 90: print("A") elif marks >= 60: print("B") else: print("C")
Step 4: Combine conditions using and.
age = 25 if age >= 18 and age <= 60: print("Working age")
Step 5: Combine conditions using or.
day = "Sunday" if day == "Saturday" or day == "Sunday": print("Weekend")
Step 6: Use not to check an empty value.
name = "" if not name: print("Name is required")
Step 7: Validate simple data.
records = [] if records: print("Processing records") else: print("No records available")
Step 8: Check for a missing value.
value = None if value is None: print("Value is missing") else: print("Value is available")
Final Understanding Check:

What happens after Python finds the first True condition? 6. Why is condition order important? 7. What is the difference between == and =? 8. What does and mean in a condition? 9. What does or mean in a condition? 10. What does not do? 11. Can a truthy or falsy value be used directly in an if statement? 12. Why is indentation important in conditional statements?
Practice Goal: You should be able to use if, elif, and else, combine conditions with logical operators, understand condition order, and apply conditions for basic data validation.

qna.q: Q12. Why is indentation important?
qna.a: Indentation defines which code belongs to the conditional block.

qna.q: Q13. Can you use a list directly in an if statement?
qna.a: Yes. A non-empty list is truthy and an empty list is falsy.

qna.q: Q14. What is a nested conditional statement?
qna.a: It is a conditional statement placed inside another conditional block.

items.title: Loops
explanation: Simple Meaning
A loop allows you to execute the same block of code repeatedly.
Simple Definition: A loop is used to repeat a block of code while iterating over data or while a condition remains true.
for i in range(3): print("Hello")
Output:
Hello Hello Hello
Start ↓ Run code ↓ Run code again ↓ Repeat until finished
Why Do We Need Loops?
Without loops, you would need to write the same code repeatedly.
Without a loop:
print("Process record") print("Process record") print("Process record")
Using a loop:
for i in range(3): print("Process record")
Key Idea: Write the code once and let the loop repeat it.
Types of Loops in Python
Python mainly provides two types of loops:
Python Loops │ ├── for loop │ └── Iterate over a sequence or collection │ └── while loop └── Repeat while a condition is True
for Loop
A for loop is used to iterate through an iterable such as a list, string, tuple, dictionary, or range.
for item in [10, 20, 30]: print(item)
Output:
10 20 30
[10, 20, 30] ↓ First item → 10 → Run code Second item → 20 → Run code Third item → 30 → Run code ↓ Finished
Understanding the for Loop Syntax
for variable in iterable: # code to repeat

PartMeaning
forStarts the loop
variableStores the current item
inConnects the variable with the iterable
iterableThe collection or sequence being iterated
:Starts the loop block
IndentationDefines the code that belongs to the loop
Looping Through a List
names = ["Nani", "Kumar", "Ravi"] for name in names: print(name)
Output:
Nani Kumar Ravi
names ↓ ["Nani", "Kumar", "Ravi"] ↓ name = "Nani" → Run name = "Kumar" → Run name = "Ravi" → Run ↓ Finished
Looping Through a String
A string can also be iterated character by character.
word = "Python" for letter in word: print(letter)
Output:
P y t h o n
Looping with range() ⭐
range() is commonly used when you want to repeat code a specific number of times.
for i in range(5): print(i)
Output:
0 1 2 3 4
Important: range(5) starts at 0 and stops before 5.
range(5) ↓ 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 ↓ Stop before 5
Different Forms of range()
range(stop) range(start, stop) range(start, stop, step)
range(stop)
for i in range(3): print(i)
Output:
0 1 2
range(start, stop)
for i in range(2, 6): print(i)
Output:
2 3 4 5
Remember: The stop value is not included.
range(start, stop, step)
for i in range(0, 10, 2): print(i)
Output:
0 2 4 6 8
Start = 0 Step = 2 Stop = 10 0 → 2 → 4 → 6 → 8 ↓ Stop before 10
while Loop
A while loop repeats a block of code as long as its condition is True.
count = 1 while count <= 3: print(count) count += 1
Output:
1 2 3
count = 1 ↓ Is count <= 3? ↓ Yes Print count ↓ Increase count ↓ Check condition again ↓ No → Stop
Understanding while Loop Syntax
while condition: # code to repeat
The condition is checked before every iteration.
Key Rule: The loop continues while the condition is True. It stops when the condition becomes False.
Why Updating the Condition Is Important ⚠️
In many while loops, you must update a value so that the condition eventually becomes False.
count = 1 while count <= 3: print(count) count += 1
If count += 1 is missing, the loop may run forever.
count = 1 ↓ Condition is True ↓ Run loop ↓ Value updated? ↙ ↘ Yes No ↓ ↓ Eventually May create stop infinite loop
Infinite Loop ⚠️
An infinite loop happens when a loop condition never becomes False.
count = 1 while count <= 3: print(count)
Here, count never changes, so count <= 3 remains true forever.
Warning: Always make sure a while loop has a way to eventually stop.
for vs while

forwhile
Iterates through an iterableRepeats while a condition is true
Useful for lists, strings, ranges, etc.Useful when repetitions depend on a condition
Usually has a clear end based on itemsMust ensure the condition eventually becomes false
Use for ↓ When iterating over data Examples: List String Dictionary range() ──────────────── Use while ↓ When repeating based on a condition Example: while count <= 10
Nested Loops
A nested loop is a loop inside another loop.
for i in range(2): for j in range(3): print(i, j)
For every iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop completes all of its iterations.
Outer Loop: i = 0 ├── j = 0 ├── j = 1 └── j = 2 Outer Loop: i = 1 ├── j = 0 ├── j = 1 └── j = 2
Looping Through a Dictionary
Dictionaries can be iterated in different ways.
student = { "name": "Nani", "age": 25 } for key in student: print(key)
This prints the dictionary keys.
for key, value in student.items(): print(key, value)
Output:
name Nani age 25
Note: Dictionaries will be covered in more detail in the Data Structures section.
Data Engineering Example ⭐
Loops are heavily used to process multiple records.
records = [ {"id": 101, "name": "Nani"}, {"id": 102, "name": "Kumar"}, {"id": 103, "name": "Ravi"} ] for record in records: print(record["id"], record["name"])
Data Records ↓ for each record ↓ Read record ↓ Process record ↓ Next record ↓ All records completed
Another Data Processing Example
sales = [100, 250, 300, 150] total = 0 for amount in sales: total += amount print(total)
Output:
800
total = 0 ↓ 100 → total = 100 ↓ 250 → total = 350 ↓ 300 → total = 650 ↓ 150 → total = 800
Common Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Forgetting the colon for i in range(5) Correct: for i in range(5): ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Incorrect indentation for i in range(3): print(i) Correct: for i in range(3): print(i) ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Expecting range(5) to include 5 range(5) Gives: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Creating an infinite while loop while count <= 3: print(count) Update count so the condition can become False.
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
for loop ↓ Repeat for each item while loop ↓ Repeat while condition is True range() ↓ Generate a sequence of numbers Stop value ↓ Usually not included
Quick Summary

ConceptKey Point
LoopRepeats a block of code
forIterates through items
whileRepeats while a condition is True
range()Generates a sequence of numbers
IndentationDefines the loop body
Nested loopA loop inside another loop
Infinite loopA loop that never stops
Final Definition: Loops allow Python to repeatedly execute code. Use for when iterating through data and while when repetition depends on a condition.
practice: Step 1: Print numbers from 0 to 4 using a for loop.
for i in range(5): print(i)
Step 2: Print numbers from 1 to 5.
for i in range(1, 6): print(i)
Step 3: Print even numbers from 0 to 10.
for i in range(0, 11, 2): print(i)
Step 4: Loop through a list.
names = ["Nani", "Kumar", "Ravi"] for name in names: print(name)
Step 5: Loop through the characters of a string.
word = "Python" for letter in word: print(letter)
Step 6: Create a while loop that prints numbers from 1 to 5.
count = 1 while count <= 5: print(count) count += 1
Step 7: Calculate the total of a list of numbers.
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40] total = 0 for number in numbers: total += number print(total)
Step 8: Process multiple records using a loop.
records = [101, 102, 103] for record in records: print("Processing record:", record)
Final Understanding Check:

1. What is a loop? 2. What is the difference between for and while? 3. When should you use a for loop? 4. When should you use a while loop? 5. What values does range(5) produce? 6. Does the stop value in range() get included? 7. Why is indentation important in loops? 8. What is an infinite loop? 9. Why should a while loop update its condition? 10. What is a nested loop? 11. How can you loop through a list? 12. How can loops be used in data processing?
Practice Goal: You should be able to use for and while loops, work with range(), iterate through basic collections, and avoid common infinite loop mistakes.

qna.q: Q1. What is a loop?
qna.a: A loop is used to repeatedly execute a block of code.

qna.q: Q2. What are the two main types of loops in Python?
qna.a: The two main types are for loops and while loops.

qna.q: Q3. When is a for loop commonly used?
qna.a: A for loop is commonly used to iterate through an iterable such as a list, string, tuple, dictionary, or range.

qna.q: Q4. When is a while loop used?
qna.a: A while loop is used when code should repeat as long as a condition remains True.

qna.q: Q5. What does range(5) produce?
qna.a: It produces the values 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4.

qna.q: Q6. Is the stop value included in range()?
qna.a: No. The stop value is not included.

qna.q: Q7. What does range(2, 6) produce?
qna.a: It produces 2, 3, 4, and 5.

qna.q: Q8. What does range(0, 10, 2) produce?
qna.a: It produces 0, 2, 4, 6, and 8.

qna.q: Q9. Why is indentation important in a loop?
qna.a: Indentation defines which code belongs to the loop and should be repeated.

qna.q: Q10. What is an infinite loop?
qna.a: An infinite loop is a loop that never stops because its stopping condition never becomes False.

qna.q: Q11. Why should you update values in many while loops?
qna.a: Values often need to be updated so the condition can eventually become False and the loop can stop.

qna.q: Q12. What is a nested loop?
qna.a: A nested loop is a loop inside another loop.

qna.q: Q13. How do you loop through a list?
qna.a: Use a for loop, for example: for item in my_list:

qna.q: Q14. What is the main difference between for and while?
qna.a: A for loop usually iterates through items, while a while loop repeats based on a condition.

qna.q: Q15. Complete: Use ______ when iterating through data and ______ when repetition depends on a condition.
qna.a: for, while

items.title: `break`, `continue`, `pass`
explanation: Simple Meaning
break, continue, and pass are Python statements used to control how code executes, especially inside loops and conditional blocks.
Simple Definition: break stops a loop, continue skips the current iteration, and pass does nothing and acts as a placeholder.
Loop or Code Block ↓ ┌──────┼──────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ break continue pass ↓ ↓ ↓ Stop Skip Do nothing loop current placeholder iteration
1. The break Statement
The break statement immediately stops the nearest loop. After break runs, Python exits the loop and continues with the code after it.
for number in range(1, 6): if number == 4: break print(number) print("Loop finished")
Output:
1 2 3 Loop finished
number = 1 → Print number = 2 → Print number = 3 → Print number = 4 → break ↓ Exit loop
When number becomes 4, the condition is true. Python executes break, so the loop stops immediately.
Using break with a while Loop
count = 1 while True: print(count) if count == 3: break count += 1
Output:
1 2 3
while True creates a loop that would normally continue forever. The break statement provides the condition for exiting it.
Key Point: break exits the entire nearest loop, not just the current iteration.
Real Example: Stop When Data Is Found ⭐
records = [101, 102, 103, 104] for record in records: if record == 103: print("Record found") break
Once the required record is found, there may be no need to continue searching.
2. The continue Statement
The continue statement skips the remaining code in the current iteration and moves to the next iteration of the loop.
for number in range(1, 6): if number == 3: continue print(number)
Output:
1 2 4 5
number = 1 → Print number = 2 → Print number = 3 → continue ↓ Skip remaining code ↓ Next iteration number = 4 → Print number = 5 → Print
When number is 3, Python does not execute print(number). It immediately starts the next iteration.
Example: Skip Invalid Data ⭐
values = [10, None, 20, None, 30] for value in values: if value is None: continue print(value)
Output:
10 20 30
Read value ↓ Is value None? ┌──Yes──→ continue → Skip processing │ No ↓ Process value
This pattern is useful when processing data and you want to skip invalid, missing, or unwanted records.
Key Point: continue does not stop the loop. It only skips the current iteration.
3. The pass Statement
The pass statement does nothing. It is used when Python requires a statement, but you do not want to write the actual code yet.
if True: pass
Without pass, an empty code block would cause a syntax error.
Using pass as a Placeholder
def process_data(): pass
The function is created successfully, but it currently has no implementation.
for number in range(1, 4): if number == 2: pass print(number)
Output:
1 2 3
Unlike break or continue, pass does not change the flow of the loop. Python simply continues normally.
Key Point: pass means: "Do nothing here for now."
Main Difference ⭐

StatementWhat It DoesLoop Continues?
breakImmediately exits the loopNo
continueSkips the current iterationYes
passDoes nothingYes, normally
Visual Comparison

break Iteration ↓ Condition? ↓ Yes STOP ENTIRE LOOP ────────────────── continue Iteration ↓ Condition? ↓ Yes SKIP CURRENT ITERATION ↓ NEXT ITERATION ────────────────── pass Code Block ↓ pass ↓ DO NOTHING ↓ CONTINUE NORMALLY
break vs continue
# break for number in range(1, 6): if number == 3: break print(number)
Output:
1 2
# continue for number in range(1, 6): if number == 3: continue print(number)
Output:
1 2 4 5
Easy Memory Rule: break = Stop. continue = Skip. pass = Nothing.
Using break in Nested Loops
A break statement exits only the nearest loop containing it.
for i in range(1, 3): for j in range(1, 4): if j == 2: break print(i, j)
Output:
1 1 2 1
When j == 2, only the inner loop stops. The outer loop continues.
Common Data Engineering Example
These statements can be useful when processing many records.
records = [100, None, 200, -1, 300] for record in records: if record is None: continue if record == -1: print("Stop signal received") break print("Processing:", record)
Output:
Processing: 100 Processing: 200 Stop signal received
Get record ↓ Is missing? Yes → continue → Next record ↓ No Is stop signal? Yes → break → Exit loop ↓ No Process record ↓ Next record
Common Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Using break when you only want to skip one item break → Stops the entire loop continue → Skips only the current iteration ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Using continue without understanding skipped code if value is None: continue print(value) The print statement will not run for None. ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Thinking pass skips an iteration pass does NOT skip anything. It simply does nothing. ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Creating an infinite while loop without a break condition while True: print("Running") This continues forever unless another exit occurs.
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
break "I'm done with this loop" ↓ Exit loop continue "Skip this item" ↓ Next iteration pass "Nothing to write here yet" ↓ Continue normally
Quick Summary

ConceptKey Point
breakImmediately exits the nearest loop
continueSkips the remaining code in the current iteration
passDoes nothing and acts as a placeholder
Nested loop + breakOnly the nearest loop is exited
while TrueOften uses break to provide an exit condition
Data processingcontinue can skip invalid records
Final Definition: break, continue, and pass are flow-control statements. break stops a loop, continue skips the current iteration, and pass performs no action and is commonly used as a placeholder.
practice: Step 1: Use break to stop a loop.
for number in range(1, 10): if number == 5: break print(number)
Step 2: Use continue to skip one value.
for number in range(1, 6): if number == 3: continue print(number)
Step 3: Skip even numbers using continue.
for number in range(1, 11): if number % 2 == 0: continue print(number)
Step 4: Use break with a while loop.
count = 1 while True: if count > 5: break print(count) count += 1
Step 5: Create an empty function using pass.
def future_function(): pass
Step 6: Skip missing values.
data = [10, None, 20, None, 30] for value in data: if value is None: continue print(value)
Step 7: Stop processing when a special value is found.
data = [10, 20, 30, -1, 40] for value in data: if value == -1: break print("Processing:", value)
Final Understanding Check:

1. What does break do? 2. What does continue do? 3. What does pass do? 4. Does break stop one iteration or the entire loop? 5. Does continue stop the loop? 6. Which statement is useful for skipping invalid data? 7. Which statement can be used to exit while True? 8. Does pass skip an iteration? 9. In nested loops, which loop does break exit? 10. Complete: break = ______ continue = ______ pass = ______
Practice Goal: You should clearly understand when to stop a loop with break, when to skip an item with continue, and when to use pass as a placeholder.

qna.q: Q1. What does break do?
qna.a: break immediately exits the nearest loop.

qna.q: Q2. What does continue do?
qna.a: continue skips the remaining code in the current iteration and moves to the next iteration.

qna.q: Q3. What does pass do?
qna.a: pass does nothing and is commonly used as a placeholder where Python requires a statement.

qna.q: Q4. Does break stop only the current iteration?
qna.a: No. break exits the entire nearest loop.

qna.q: Q5. Does continue stop a loop?
qna.a: No. It skips only the current iteration and the loop continues.

qna.q: Q6. Does pass skip an iteration?
qna.a: No. pass does nothing, and execution continues normally.

qna.q: Q7. Which statement is useful for skipping invalid records during data processing?
qna.a: continue is commonly used to skip invalid or unwanted records.

qna.q: Q8. How can you exit a while True loop?
qna.a: You can use break when the required exit condition is met.

qna.q: Q9. What happens when break is used inside nested loops?
qna.a: It exits only the nearest loop containing the break statement.

qna.q: Q10. Why is pass useful?
qna.a: It allows you to create an intentionally empty code block without causing a syntax error.

qna.q: Q11. Which statement should you use if you want to ignore one item but continue processing the remaining items?
qna.a: continue.

qna.q: Q12. Which statement should you use if you want to completely stop searching after finding a required value?
qna.a: break.

qna.q: Q13. What is the easiest memory rule for these three statements?
qna.a: break = Stop, continue = Skip, pass = Do nothing.

qna.q: Q14. Can break and continue be used to control loop execution?
qna.a: Yes. break stops a loop and continue skips the current iteration.

qna.q: Q15. Complete: break = ______, continue = ______, pass = ______.
qna.a: stop, skip, do nothing

items.title: Lists
explanation: Simple Meaning
A list is a Python data structure used to store multiple values in a single variable.
Simple Definition: A list is an ordered, mutable collection that can contain multiple values, including values of different data types.
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40] print(numbers)
Output:
[10, 20, 30, 40]
List ↓ [10, 20, 30, 40] │ │ │ │ ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ Item Item Item Item 0 1 2 3
Creating a List
Lists are created using square brackets []. Items are separated by commas.
names = ["Nani", "Kumar", "Ravi"] ages = [20, 25, 30] mixed = [10, "Python", True, 3.14]
A list can contain values of different types.
Important: An empty list is created using [].
records = [] print(records)
Output:
[]
List Characteristics ⭐
Python List │ ├── Ordered ├── Mutable ├── Allows duplicates ├── Allows different data types └── Zero-indexed
1. Lists Are Ordered
List items maintain their order. The position of each item can be accessed using its index.
colors = ["red", "green", "blue"] print(colors)
The order remains:
Index 0 1 2 ↓ ↓ ↓ red → green → blue
2. Lists Are Mutable ⭐
Mutable means that you can change, add, or remove items after the list has been created.
numbers = [10, 20, 30] numbers[1] = 200 print(numbers)
Output:
[10, 200, 30]
Key Point: Lists can be modified after creation.
3. Lists Allow Duplicate Values
numbers = [10, 20, 10, 30, 10] print(numbers)
Output:
[10, 20, 10, 30, 10]
Duplicate values are allowed in lists.
Accessing List Items
List items are accessed using their index. Python uses zero-based indexing.
names = ["Nani", "Kumar", "Ravi"] print(names[0]) print(names[1]) print(names[2])
Output:
Nani Kumar Ravi
names = ["Nani", "Kumar", "Ravi"] Index: 0 1 2 ↓ ↓ ↓ Value: Nani Kumar Ravi
Remember: The first list item has index 0, not 1.
Negative Indexing
Python also allows negative indexes to access items from the end of the list.
names = ["Nani", "Kumar", "Ravi"] print(names[-1]) print(names[-2]) print(names[-3])
Output:
Ravi Kumar Nani
Positive index: 0 1 2 ↓ ↓ ↓ Nani → Kumar → Ravi ↑ ↑ -3 -1
List Slicing
Slicing is used to extract a portion of a list.
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50] print(numbers[1:4])
Output:
[20, 30, 40]
Important: In list[start:stop], the start index is included and the stop index is excluded.
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50] 0 1 2 3 4 ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ 10 20 30 40 50 numbers[1:4] ↓ 20, 30, 40 Stop before index 4
Changing List Items
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "orange"] fruits[1] = "mango" print(fruits)
Output:
['apple', 'mango', 'orange']
Changing Multiple Items
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40] numbers[1:3] = [200, 300] print(numbers)
Output:
[10, 200, 300, 40]
Adding Items to a List
append()
append() adds one item to the end of a list.
numbers = [10, 20, 30] numbers.append(40) print(numbers)
Output:
[10, 20, 30, 40]
[10, 20, 30] ↓ append(40) [10, 20, 30, 40]
insert()
insert() adds an item at a specific index.
numbers = [10, 20, 30] numbers.insert(1, 15) print(numbers)
Output:
[10, 15, 20, 30]
extend()
extend() adds multiple items from another iterable to the end of the list.
numbers = [10, 20] numbers.extend([30, 40]) print(numbers)
Output:
[10, 20, 30, 40]
Removing Items
remove()
remove() removes the first occurrence of a specified value.
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 20] numbers.remove(20) print(numbers)
Output:
[10, 30, 20]
Important: remove() works with a value, not an index.
pop()
pop() removes and returns an item using its index. If no index is supplied, it removes the last item.
numbers = [10, 20, 30] value = numbers.pop() print(value) print(numbers)
Output:
30 [10, 20]
You can also specify an index:
numbers = [10, 20, 30] numbers.pop(1) print(numbers)
Output:
[10, 30]
del
del can remove an item or a slice from a list.
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40] del numbers[1] print(numbers)
Output:
[10, 30, 40]
clear()
clear() removes all items from the list but keeps the list itself.
numbers = [10, 20, 30] numbers.clear() print(numbers)
Output:
[]
Useful List Functions
len()
len() returns the number of items in a list.
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40] print(len(numbers))
Output:
4
min(), max(), and sum()
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40] print(min(numbers)) print(max(numbers)) print(sum(numbers))
Output:
10 40 100
Note: sum(), min(), and max() are useful for numeric lists.
Checking Whether an Item Exists
The in operator checks whether a value exists in a list.
names = ["Nani", "Kumar", "Ravi"] print("Nani" in names) print("John" in names)
Output:
True False
Looping Through a List
A for loop can be used to process every item in a list.
numbers = [10, 20, 30] for number in numbers: print(number)
Output:
10 20 30
List ↓ [10, 20, 30] ↓ for each item ↓ Process item ↓ Next item ↓ Finished
Using enumerate()
enumerate() allows you to get both the index and the value while looping through a list.
names = ["Nani", "Kumar", "Ravi"] for index, name in enumerate(names): print(index, name)
Output:
0 Nani 1 Kumar 2 Ravi
Note: enumerate() will be covered more deeply in the Built-in Functions section, but you should recognize its basic use here.
Sorting a List
sort() modifies the existing list and sorts its items.
numbers = [30, 10, 20] numbers.sort() print(numbers)
Output:
[10, 20, 30]
For descending order:
numbers = [30, 10, 20] numbers.sort(reverse=True) print(numbers)
Output:
[30, 20, 10]
sorted() vs sort()
sort() changes the original list, while sorted() returns a new sorted list.
numbers = [30, 10, 20] new_numbers = sorted(numbers) print(numbers) print(new_numbers)
Output:
[30, 10, 20] [10, 20, 30]
Remember: sort() modifies the original list. sorted() creates a sorted result without changing the original list.
Copying Lists ⚠️
Assigning one list variable to another does not create an independent copy.
numbers = [10, 20, 30] other = numbers other.append(40) print(numbers)
Output:
[10, 20, 30, 40]
Both variables refer to the same list.
numbers ─────┐ ↓ [10, 20, 30] ↑ other ───────┘ Same list object
To create a shallow copy:
numbers = [10, 20, 30] other = numbers.copy() other.append(40) print(numbers) print(other)
Output:
Nested Lists
A list can contain other lists. This is called a nested list.
matrix = [ [1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9] ] print(matrix[0]) print(matrix[1][2])
Output:
[1, 2, 3] 6
Nested lists will be used later when working with more complex data structures.
Lists in Data Engineering ⭐
Lists are frequently used to temporarily hold records, IDs, file names, API results, columns, or values that need to be processed.
file_names = [ "sales.csv", "customers.csv", "products.csv" ] for file_name in file_names: print("Processing:", file_name)
Output:
Processing: sales.csv Processing: customers.csv Processing: products.csv
File names ↓ List ↓ for each file ↓ Read / process file ↓ Next file
Example: Collecting Valid Records
values = [10, None, 20, None, 30] valid_values = [] for value in values: if value is not None: valid_values.append(value) print(valid_values)
Output:
[10, 20, 30]
Data Engineering Connection: Lists are useful when collecting records or intermediate values during ETL and data-processing operations.
Common Mistakes ⚠️

Mistake 1 ❌ Forgetting zero-based indexing list[1] is the SECOND item, not the first. ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Using remove() with an index remove(2) → removes value 2 pop(2) → removes item at index 2 ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Using append() when you want to add multiple items numbers.append([3, 4]) → [1, 2, [3, 4]] numbers.extend([3, 4]) → [1, 2, 3, 4] ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Accidentally sharing the same list other = numbers Use numbers.copy() when an independent shallow copy is needed. ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Accessing an index that does not exist numbers = [10, 20] numbers[2] This raises IndexError.
Easy Memory Rule 🧠
List ↓ Ordered + Mutable Access ↓ list[index] Add ↓ append() / insert() / extend() Remove ↓ remove() / pop() / del / clear() Check ↓ in Count ↓ len() Loop ↓ for item in list
Quick Summary

ConceptKey Point
ListOrdered, mutable collection
IndexStarts from 0
Negative indexAccesses items from the end
SlicingExtracts part of a list
append()Adds one item to the end
insert()Adds an item at an index
extend()Adds multiple items
remove()Removes the first matching value
pop()Removes an item by index and returns it
clear()Removes all items
len()Returns number of items
inChecks membership
sort()Sorts the original list
sorted()Returns a sorted result
copy()Creates a shallow copy

Final Definition: A Python list is an ordered and mutable collection used to store multiple values. Lists support indexing, slicing, adding and removing items, iteration, and modification, making them one of the most commonly used data structures in Python.
practice: Step 1: Create a list containing five numbers and print it.
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50] print(numbers)
Step 2: Access the first, third, and last items.
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50] print(numbers[0]) print(numbers[2]) print(numbers[-1])
Step 3: Change one item in a list.
numbers = [10, 20, 30] numbers[1] = 200 print(numbers)
Step 4: Add values using append(), insert(), and extend().
numbers = [10, 20] numbers.append(30) numbers.insert(1, 15) numbers.extend([40, 50]) print(numbers)
Step 5: Remove values using remove() and pop().
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40] numbers.remove(20) numbers.pop() print(numbers)
Step 6: Check whether a value exists in a list.
names = ["Nani", "Kumar", "Ravi"] if "Nani" in names: print("Name found")
Step 7: Loop through a list and process every value.
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40] for number in numbers: print(number * 2)
Step 8: Calculate the total of a list.
sales = [100, 200, 300, 400] total = sum(sales) print(total)
Step 9: Create a new list containing only valid values.
values = [10, None, 20, None, 30] valid_values = [] for value in values: if value is not None: valid_values.append(value) print(valid_values)
Step 10: Practice copying a list.
numbers = [10, 20, 30] copy_numbers = numbers.copy() copy_numbers.append(40) print(numbers) print(copy_numbers)
Final Understanding Check:

1. What is a list? 2. Why are lists called mutable? 3. What index does the first item have? 4. What does negative index -1 mean? 5. What is list slicing? 6. What does append() do? 7. What is the difference between append() and extend()? 8. What is the difference between remove() and pop()? 9. What does len() return? 10. How do you check whether an item exists in a list? 11. What is the difference between sort() and sorted()? 12. Why can other = numbers be dangerous when you want an independent list? 13. What does copy() do? 14. How can you loop through a list? 15. Why are lists useful in data engineering?
Practice Goal: You should be able to create, access, modify, add, remove, search, sort, copy, and iterate through Python lists, and understand how lists are used when processing data.

items.title: Tuples
explanation: What is a Tuple?
A tuple is an ordered collection of Python objects that is immutable, meaning its elements cannot be changed after the tuple is created.
Tuples are similar to lists, but the main difference is that lists are mutable while tuples are immutable.
numbers = (10, 20, 30, 40) print(numbers)
Definition: A tuple is an ordered, immutable collection that can store multiple values, including duplicate values and values of different data types.
Tuple vs List

FeatureListTuple
Syntax[]()
OrderedYesYes
MutableYesNo
DuplicatesAllowedAllowed
Different data typesAllowedAllowed
Can be changed after creationYesNo
LIST → Ordered + Mutable TUPLE → Ordered + Immutable
Creating a Tuple
The most common way to create a tuple is by using parentheses.
numbers = (10, 20, 30) names = ("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie") mixed = (10, "Python", 3.14, True) print(numbers) print(mixed)
Tuples can contain values of different data types.
Empty Tuple
empty = () print(empty)
An empty pair of parentheses creates an empty tuple.
Single-Element Tuple
A single-element tuple requires a trailing comma.
x = (10,) print(type(x))
Without the comma, Python treats the parentheses as normal grouping parentheses.
x = (10) print(type(x)) # int y = (10,) print(type(y)) # tuple
Memory Rule: One value + comma = single-element tuple.
Creating Tuples Without Parentheses
Python also supports tuple packing without explicitly writing parentheses.
data = 10, 20, 30 print(data) print(type(data))
The comma is what creates the tuple structure here.
Tuple Indexing
Tuples are ordered, so each element has an index starting from 0.
numbers = (10, 20, 30, 40) print(numbers[0]) print(numbers[1]) print(numbers[3])
Tuple: (10, 20, 30, 40) Index: 0 1 2 3 Negative: -4 -3 -2 -1
Negative Indexing
Negative indexes access elements from the end of the tuple.
numbers = (10, 20, 30, 40) print(numbers[-1]) # 40 print(numbers[-2]) # 30 print(numbers[-4]) # 10
Tuple Slicing
Slicing allows you to retrieve a portion of a tuple.
numbers = (10, 20, 30, 40, 50) print(numbers[1:4]) print(numbers[:3]) print(numbers[2:]) print(numbers[::2])
The original tuple is not modified. Slicing creates another tuple.
Tuples Are Immutable
The most important property of tuples is immutability. You cannot directly change, add, or remove elements after creation.
numbers = (10, 20, 30) numbers[0] = 100 # TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment
This is the major difference from lists.
numbers = [10, 20, 30] numbers[0] = 100 print(numbers) # [100, 20, 30]
Important: You cannot modify the structure or replace individual elements of an ordinary tuple after it has been created.
Adding or Removing Tuple Elements
Tuples do not have methods such as append(), insert(), remove(), or pop() because tuples cannot be structurally modified.
data = (10, 20, 30) # data.append(40) # AttributeError # data.remove(20) # AttributeError
If you really need to modify the values, you can create a new tuple.
data = (10, 20, 30) data = data + (40,) print(data)
Tuple Concatenation
You can combine tuples using the + operator.
a = (1, 2, 3) b = (4, 5, 6) result = a + b print(result)
This does not modify either original tuple. A new tuple is created.
Tuple Repetition
The * operator can repeat the contents of a tuple.
numbers = (1, 2) result = numbers * 3 print(result)
Output:
(1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2)
Checking Membership
Use in and not in to check whether a value exists in a tuple.
parts = ("CPU", "RAM", "SSD") print("RAM" in parts) print("GPU" not in parts)
This is useful when checking whether a known value exists in a fixed collection.
Length of a Tuple
Use len() to find the number of elements.
data = (10, 20, 30, 40) print(len(data))
Looping Through a Tuple
Because tuples are iterable, you can use a for loop to process each element.
parts = ("CPU", "RAM", "SSD") for part in parts: print(part)
You can also use enumerate() when you need both the index and value.
parts = ("CPU", "RAM", "SSD") for index, part in enumerate(parts): print(index, part)
Useful Tuple Methods
Tuples have fewer methods than lists because they cannot be modified.
numbers = (10, 20, 20, 30, 20) print(numbers.count(20)) print(numbers.index(30))

MethodPurpose
count()Counts how many times a value occurs
index()Returns the index of the first matching value
Built-in Functions with Tuples
Several Python built-in functions work directly with tuples.
numbers = (10, 20, 30, 40) print(len(numbers)) print(min(numbers)) print(max(numbers)) print(sum(numbers))
These functions are particularly useful when working with numerical records.
Tuple Unpacking
Tuple unpacking assigns tuple elements to multiple variables in one statement.
person = ("John", 25, "India") name, age, country = person print(name) print(age) print(country)
("John", 25, "India") ↓ ↓ ↓ name age country
The number of variables should normally match the number of values.
Using * During Unpacking
The * operator can collect multiple remaining values into a list during unpacking.
numbers = (10, 20, 30, 40, 50) first, *middle, last = numbers print(first) print(middle) print(last)
This is useful when the number of middle values is variable.
Nested Tuples
A tuple can contain another tuple as an element.
data = ((1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6)) print(data[0]) print(data[1][0])
Nested structures are useful for representing grouped or fixed records.
Tuple Containing Mutable Objects
A tuple itself is immutable, but it can contain mutable objects such as lists. The list inside the tuple can still be modified.
data = ([10, 20], "Python") data[0].append(30) print(data)
Important: Tuple immutability prevents changing the tuple's elements themselves. It does not make mutable objects stored inside the tuple immutable.
Converting Between List and Tuple
You can convert a list to a tuple using tuple() and a tuple to a list using list().
numbers_list = [10, 20, 30] numbers_tuple = tuple(numbers_list) print(numbers_tuple) numbers_list_again = list(numbers_tuple) print(numbers_list_again)
This can be useful when data needs to temporarily become mutable or immutable.
Why Use Tuples?
Use a tuple when the collection represents a group of values that should not normally be changed.
database_config = ("localhost", 5432, "sales_db") host, port, database = database_config
Here, the values form one fixed configuration record. A tuple communicates that the structure is not intended to be modified.
Tuples in Data Engineering
Tuples are useful in Data Engineering for representing fixed records, coordinates, configuration values, and groups of related values while iterating through data.
record = (101, "Laptop", 25) product_id, product_name, quantity = record print(product_id) print(product_name) print(quantity)
Another common example is processing database-style rows returned by Python database libraries.
rows = [ (101, "Laptop", 25), (102, "Monitor", 10), (103, "Keyboard", 50) ] for product_id, product_name, quantity in rows: print(product_id, product_name, quantity)
Data Engineering Connection: Tuples are especially useful for fixed row-like records where the position of each value has a defined meaning.
Tuple vs List: When to Choose Which?

RequirementUse
Data needs to change frequentlyList
Data should remain fixedTuple
Need append/remove operationsList
Represent a fixed recordTuple
Represent a collection that will be modifiedList
Common Mistakes
# Mistake 1: Forgetting the comma x = (10) print(type(x)) # Correct x = (10,) print(type(x))
# Mistake 2: Trying to modify a tuple numbers = (10, 20, 30) # numbers[0] = 100
# Mistake 3: Trying to use list methods numbers = (10, 20, 30) # numbers.append(40)
Quick Memory Rule
LIST → [ ] → Mutable → Can change TUPLE → ( ) → Immutable → Cannot change
Remember: If the data represents a fixed group of values, a tuple is often a good choice. If the collection needs frequent modifications, use a list.
Summary

• Tuples are ordered collections.
  • Tuples are immutable.
  • Tuple indexes start at 0.
  • Negative indexing starts from -1.
  • Tuples support slicing.
  • Duplicates are allowed.
  • Tuples can contain different data types.
  • A single-element tuple requires a trailing comma.
  • Tuples support iteration and membership checking.
  • Useful tuple methods include count() and index().
  • Tuple unpacking is useful for working with fixed records.
  • Tuples are commonly useful for fixed row-like data in Data Engineering.
practice: Step 1: Create a tuple containing 5 numbers and print the tuple.
numbers = (10, 20, 30, 40, 50) print(numbers)
Step 2: Print the first, third, and last elements using indexing.
print(numbers[0]) print(numbers[2]) print(numbers[-1])
Step 3: Print a slice containing the second through fourth elements.
print(numbers[1:4])
Step 4: Create a single-element tuple and verify its type.
value = (100,) print(type(value))
Step 5: Create a tuple of product information and unpack it into variables.
product = (101, "Laptop", 25) product_id, product_name, quantity = product print(product_id) print(product_name) print(quantity)
Step 6: Create three tuples and combine them into one tuple.
a = (1, 2) b = (3, 4) c = (5, 6) result = a + b + c print(result)
Step 7: Create a tuple containing duplicate values and use count() and index().
data = (10, 20, 20, 30, 20) print(data.count(20)) print(data.index(30))
Step 8: Create a list of database-style rows as tuples and loop through them using tuple unpacking.
rows = [ (101, "Laptop", 25), (102, "Monitor", 10), (103, "Keyboard", 50) ] for product_id, product_name, quantity in rows: print(product_id, product_name, quantity)
Step 9: Convert a list into a tuple and then convert the tuple back into a list.
data = [10, 20, 30] t = tuple(data) print(t) new_data = list(t) print(new_data)
Step 10: Try changing an element of a tuple and observe the error. Then explain why the error occurs.
numbers = (10, 20, 30) # numbers[0] = 100
Practice Goal: Be able to create, access, slice, unpack, iterate through, and choose tuples correctly when working with fixed groups of data.
