It is important to distinguish between modifying an object and reassigning a variable.

text = "python"

text = text.upper()
The expression text.upper() creates a new string. Then the variable text is reassigned to that new string.
replace() and Immutability

text = "I like Python"

new_text = text.replace("Python", "SQL")

print(text)
# I like Python

print(new_text)
# I like SQL
The original string remains unchanged.
strip() and Immutability

text = " Python "

cleaned = text.strip()

print(text)
# Python

print(cleaned)
# Python
Data Engineering Connection: When cleaning raw text, operations such as strip(), lower(), and replace() produce transformed strings. Store the result if you need the cleaned value later.
Index Assignment Does Not Work

name = "John"

name[0] = "B"
This raises TypeError. You cannot directly replace the first character of a string.
How to Create a Modified String
You can create a new string using slicing and concatenation.

name = "John"

name = "B" + name[1:]

print(name)
# Bohn
Here, the original string is not modified. A new string is constructed.
Another Example

text = "Python"

new_text = text[:2] + "XX" + text[4:]

print(new_text)
# PyXXon
The original text remains "Python".
Strings vs Lists

FeatureStringList
MutableNoYes
Change item by indexNot allowedAllowed
Supports slicingYesYes
Methods can return new objectsYesSome methods modify the list
Example: String vs List Modification

# String
text = "Python"
# text[0] = "J" # TypeError

# List
languages = ["Python", "Java"]
languages[0] = "SQL"

print(languages)
# ['SQL', 'Java']
Why Immutability Can Be Useful
Immutability provides predictable behavior because an existing string cannot unexpectedly change through a character assignment.
It also allows strings to be safely reused and passed between different parts of a program without those parts directly changing the same string object.
String Concatenation Creates a New String

first = "Data"
second = "Engineering"

result = first + " " + second

print(first)
# Data
print(second)
# Engineering
print(result)
# Data Engineering
The concatenation operation creates a new string rather than changing first or second.
String Immutability in Data Engineering
Data pipelines frequently receive raw text that needs normalization. Because strings are immutable, each transformation produces a new value.

raw_value = " COMPLETED "

clean_value = raw_value.strip().lower()

print(raw_value)
# COMPLETED

print(clean_value)
# completed
This makes it clear that the raw value and cleaned value can be kept separately when required.
Example: Cleaning a Data Record

raw_record = " EMP001, JOHN DOE , COMPLETED "

parts = raw_record.split(",")

employee_id = parts[0].strip()
name = parts[1].strip().title()
status = parts[2].strip().lower()

print(employee_id)
# EMP001
print(name)
# John Doe
print(status)
# completed
Each string transformation creates a new string value. The original raw record remains unchanged.
Important Mental Model

Immutable String
│
▼
Original value cannot change
│
▼
Operation creates a new string
│
▼
Variable can reference the new string
Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Trying to assign a character using text[index] = value.

Mistake 2: Assuming upper(), replace(), or strip() changes the original string.

Mistake 3: Calling a string method without storing its result when the transformed value is needed later.

Mistake 4: Confusing reassignment of a variable with modification of the original string object.
Key Takeaway

Python strings are immutable. You cannot change individual characters or modify an existing string in place. String operations create new strings, and reassignment can make a variable refer to the new value.
practice: Step 1: Try to change the first character of a string and observe the error.

text = "Python"

text[0] = "J"
Step 2: Use upper() and verify that the original string is unchanged.

text = "python"

result = text.upper()

print(text)
print(result)
Step 3: Use replace() to create a new string.

text = "I am learning Python"

new_text = text.replace("Python", "SQL")

print(text)
print(new_text)
Step 4: Clean a string without modifying the original value.

raw_data = " Bangalore "

clean_data = raw_data.strip()

print(raw_data)
print(clean_data)
Step 5: Create a new string by replacing the first character using slicing and concatenation.

text = "Python"

new_text = "J" + text[1:]

print(new_text)
# Jython
Step 6: Create a new string by replacing a portion of a string using slicing.

text = "Python"

new_text = text[:2] + "XX" + text[4:]

print(new_text)
Step 7: Build a simple data-cleaning transformation and preserve both raw and cleaned values.

raw_status = " COMPLETED "

clean_status = raw_status.strip().lower()

print("Raw:", raw_status)
print("Clean:", clean_status)
Step 8: Explain why the following code does not modify the original string.

name = "john"
name.upper()
print(name)
Step 9: Compare string immutability with list mutability.

text = "Python"
numbers = [10, 20, 30]

# Try changing both using an index.
# Observe the difference.
Step 10: Process a raw record while keeping the original record unchanged.

raw_record = " EMP001, JOHN DOE , COMPLETED "

parts = raw_record.split(",")

employee_id = parts[0].strip()
name = parts[1].strip().title()
status = parts[2].strip().lower()

print("Raw:", raw_record)
print("Clean:", employee_id, name, status)

Practice Goal: Understand that strings cannot be changed in place. Be able to recognize when a new string is created, store transformed values correctly, and explain the difference between object modification and variable reassignment.

qna.q: Q1. What does immutable mean in Python?
qna.a: Immutable means that an existing object cannot be changed after it has been created.

qna.q: Q2. Are Python strings mutable or immutable?
qna.a: Python strings are immutable.

qna.q: Q3. Can you change a character of a string using its index?
qna.a: No. An expression such as text[0] = "J" raises a TypeError.

qna.q: Q4. Do string methods modify the original string?
qna.a: No. Methods such as upper(), lower(), replace(), and strip() return new strings.

qna.q: Q5. What happens when you execute text = text.upper()?
qna.a: upper() creates a new string, and the variable text is reassigned to reference that new string.

qna.q: Q6. Does reassignment violate string immutability?
qna.a: No. Reassignment changes which object a variable references; it does not modify the existing string object.

qna.q: Q7. How can you create a modified version of a string?
qna.a: You can use string methods, slicing, concatenation, or other operations to create a new string.

qna.q: Q8. Why does text.upper() not change text automatically?
qna.a: Because upper() returns a new string and does not modify the existing string.

qna.q: Q9. What happens when you use replace() on a string?
qna.a: replace() returns a new string containing the requested replacements while leaving the original string unchanged.

qna.q: Q10. Are strings and lists both immutable?
qna.a: No. Strings are immutable, while lists are mutable.

qna.q: Q11. Why can numbers[0] = 100 work for a list but text[0] = "J" fail for a string?
qna.a: Lists are mutable and allow elements to be changed by index. Strings are immutable and do not allow character assignment.

qna.q: Q12. What is the difference between modification and reassignment?
qna.a: Modification changes an existing mutable object. Reassignment makes a variable reference a different object.

qna.q: Q13. Why is string immutability useful when processing data?
qna.a: It means an existing string value cannot be changed unexpectedly. Transformations produce separate string values.

qna.q: Q14. How can you replace the first character of a string?
qna.a: Create a new string using slicing and concatenation, for example: new_text = "J" + text[1:].

qna.q: Q15. Does string concatenation modify the original strings?
qna.a: No. Concatenation creates a new string.

qna.q: Q16. What happens to the original string after text = text.strip()?
qna.a: The original string object is not modified. The variable is reassigned to the new stripped string.

qna.q: Q17. Can string slicing modify the original string?
qna.a: No. Slicing creates a new string containing the selected characters.

qna.q: Q18. Why should you store the result of a string method?
qna.a: Because the method usually returns a new string. If you need that transformed value later, assign it to a variable.

qna.q: Q19. How is immutability relevant to Data Engineering?
qna.a: Raw text can be preserved while cleaned or normalized versions are created separately during data-processing steps.

qna.q: Q20. What is the main rule to remember about Python strings?
qna.a: You cannot modify an existing string in place; string operations create new strings.

items.title: Escape Characters
explanation: What are Escape Characters?
Escape characters are special character sequences used inside Python strings to represent characters that are difficult or impossible to type directly in a string.
Definition: An escape sequence begins with a backslash (\) and is interpreted by Python as a special character or character combination.
Basic Syntax
"text\ntext"
Here, \n does not represent two ordinary characters. Python interprets it as a newline.

Backslash (\)
│
▼
Escape sequence
│
├── \n → New line
├── \t → Tab
├── \\ → Backslash
└── \" → Double quote
1. Newline — \n
\n moves the output to a new line.

print("Hello\nWorld")

# Hello
# World
This is useful when you need multiple lines inside one string.
\t inserts a tab space.

print("Name\tAge")
print("John\t25")

# Name Age
# John 25
Data Engineering Use: Tabs can be useful when producing simple structured console output or readable logs.
3. Backslash — \\
Because the backslash starts an escape sequence, you need \\ when you want an actual backslash character inside a string.

path = "C:\\Users\\John\\data"

print(path)
# C:\Users\John\data
4. Double Quote — \"
If a string is surrounded by double quotes and you need a double quote inside it, you can escape it using \".

text = "He said \"Hello\""

print(text)
# He said "Hello"
5. Single Quote — \'
Similarly, \' represents a single quote.

text = 'It\'s Python'

print(text)
# It's Python
Using Different Quote Types
You can often avoid escaping by using the other quote type around the string.

text1 = "It's Python"
text2 = 'He said "Hello"'

print(text1)
print(text2)
This is usually easier to read than adding unnecessary escape characters.
6. Carriage Return — \r
\r moves the cursor back to the beginning of the current line.
print("Hello\rWorld")
The exact visible result can depend on the terminal or environment. It is less commonly needed in beginner Data Engineering code than \n and \t.
7. Backspace — \b
\b represents a backspace character.

text = "ABC\bD"
print(text)
Its visible behavior can vary depending on the terminal or output environment, so it is not commonly used in normal data-processing code.
8. Form Feed — \f
\f represents a form-feed character. It is uncommon in modern Data Engineering applications.

text = "Hello\fWorld"
print(text)
9. Vertical Tab — \v
\v represents a vertical tab character. Like \f, it is rarely required in everyday Python data-processing code.
10. Alert / Bell — \a
\a represents the ASCII alert or bell character.
print("Warning\a")
Whether you hear or see an alert depends on the environment.
Common Escape Sequences

Escape SequenceMeaningCommon Use
\nNewlineMulti-line output
\tTabFormatting output
\\BackslashFile paths
\"Double quoteQuotes inside double-quoted strings
\'Single quoteQuotes inside single-quoted strings
\rCarriage returnSpecial text output
\bBackspaceSpecial character output
\fForm feedRare
\vVertical tabRare
\aAlert/BellRare
Escape Characters in File Paths
Windows paths are a common place where beginners encounter escape-character problems.

path = "C:\new_folder\data"
print(path)
The sequence \n is interpreted as a newline, so a Windows path containing a folder such as \new_folder can produce unexpected output.
Using Raw Strings
A raw string treats backslashes largely as literal backslashes instead of interpreting ordinary escape sequences.

path = r"C:\new_folder\data"

print(path)
# C:\new_folder\data

Important: Raw strings are especially useful for Windows paths and regular expressions. They do not mean that every possible backslash sequence becomes unrestricted literal text, so they still have syntax rules of their own.
Escape Characters in Data Engineering
Escape characters are useful when handling raw text, generating logs, formatting output, working with file paths, and constructing text-based data.

record = "EMP001\tJohn Doe\tBangalore\tCompleted"

print(record)

# EMP001 John Doe Bangalore Completed
Creating Multi-Line Output

message = "Pipeline Status --------------- Status: SUCCESS Records: 1000"

print(message)
This can be useful for readable console messages during development or simple pipeline debugging.
Escape Characters and CSV-Like Text
When text contains quotes or separators, escape sequences can help represent the text correctly.

record = "101,\"John Doe\",Bangalore"

print(record)
# 101,"John Doe",Bangalore
For real CSV processing, use Python's csv module or later Data Engineering tools rather than manually handling every CSV escaping rule.
Escape Characters vs Raw Strings

ApproachExamplePurpose
Escape sequence"Hello\nWorld"Create special characters
Raw stringr"C:\data\files"Treat backslashes as literal characters in common cases
Escape Sequence vs Normal Character

print("Hello\nWorld")

# Two characters are written in source:
# \ and n
# But Python interprets them as one newline character.
The backslash changes how Python interprets the following character.
Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Forgetting that \n creates a newline.

Mistake 2: Writing Windows paths without considering backslash escape sequences.

Mistake 3: Using \ when you actually need an ordinary backslash and forgetting to escape it.

Mistake 4: Escaping quotes unnecessarily when using the opposite quote type would make the code clearer.

Mistake 5: Manually implementing complex CSV escaping instead of using an appropriate parser.
Key Takeaway

Remember the most useful escape sequences first: \n for newline, \t for tab, \\ for a backslash, and \" or \' for quotes. Raw strings are particularly useful when working with paths and regular expressions.
practice: Step 1: Print two words on separate lines using \n.
print("Data\nEngineering")
Step 2: Create a simple table-like output using \t.

print("Name\tAge\tCity")
print("John\t25\tBangalore")
print("Ravi\t28\tHyderabad")
Step 3: Print a Windows file path correctly using escaped backslashes.

path = "C:\\Users\\John\\data\\input.csv"

print(path)
Step 4: Print the same Windows path using a raw string.

path = r"C:\Users\John\data\input.csv"

print(path)
Step 5: Create a string containing double quotes.

text = "He said \"Data Engineering is interesting\""

print(text)
Step 6: Create a string containing an apostrophe without using an unnecessary escape character.

text = "It's time to learn Python"

print(text)
Step 7: Create a multi-line pipeline status message.

message = "Pipeline Status Status: SUCCESS Records Processed: 5000 Duration: 12 seconds"

print(message)
Step 8: Create a tab-separated record that contains employee ID, name, department, and status.

record = "EMP001\tJohn Doe\tIT\tCompleted"

print(record)
Step 9: Identify what Python will interpret in the following string and explain why the raw string version behaves differently.

path1 = "C:\\new\\test"
path2 = r"C:\new\test"

print(path1)
print(path2)
Step 10: Build a simple log message using newline and tab escape sequences.

log = "Pipeline Run Status: SUCCESS Records: 1000 Source: API"

print(log)

Practice Goal: Be able to recognize and correctly use \n, \t, \\, quote escapes, and raw strings. You should also understand why escape handling matters when working with file paths, logs, and raw data.

qna.q: Q1. What is an escape character in Python?
qna.a: An escape character is part of an escape sequence, usually beginning with a backslash, that represents a special character or character combination.

qna.q: Q2. What does \n represent?
qna.a: It represents a newline.

qna.q: Q3. What does \t represent?
qna.a: It represents a tab character.

qna.q: Q4. How do you represent a backslash inside a normal Python string?
qna.a: Use two backslashes: \\.

qna.q: Q5. How do you include a double quote inside a double-quoted string?
qna.a: Use an escaped double quote, such as \".

qna.q: Q6. How do you include an apostrophe inside a single-quoted string?
qna.a: Use an escaped single quote, such as \'.

qna.q: Q7. Can you avoid escaping quotes in some situations?
qna.a: Yes. You can often use the opposite type of quote around the string.

qna.q: Q8. What is a raw string?
qna.a: A raw string is a string literal prefixed with r where common backslash escape sequences are generally treated as literal backslashes.

qna.q: Q9. Why are raw strings useful for Windows paths?
qna.a: Windows paths contain backslashes, and raw strings can make those paths easier to write without accidentally creating escape sequences such as \n or \t.

qna.q: Q10. What problem can occur with a path such as "C:\\new\\data" if backslashes are not handled correctly?
qna.a: Sequences such as \n can be interpreted as escape sequences instead of literal backslash characters, producing unexpected results.

qna.q: Q11. What does \r represent?
qna.a: It represents a carriage return.

qna.q: Q12. What does \b represent?
qna.a: It represents a backspace character.

qna.q: Q13. What does \\ represent?
qna.a: It represents one literal backslash character.

qna.q: Q14. Are escape sequences useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: Yes. They are useful for formatting logs and output, representing file paths, handling text, and working with structured or semi-structured text.

qna.q: Q15. How can you create multiple lines inside one string?
qna.a: You can use the newline escape sequence \n or use a multi-line string literal.

qna.q: Q16. What is the difference between \n and \t?
qna.a: \n moves to a new line, while \t inserts a tab character.

qna.q: Q17. Should you manually handle all CSV escaping with string replacement?
qna.a: No. For real CSV processing, use Python's csv module or an appropriate data-processing library.

qna.q: Q18. What is the purpose of the backslash in an escape sequence?
qna.a: It tells Python that the following character or sequence should be interpreted specially.

qna.q: Q19. Are \f and \v commonly required in Data Engineering?
qna.a: No. They are valid escape sequences but are rarely needed in everyday Data Engineering work.

qna.q: Q20. Which escape sequences should a beginner remember first?
qna.a: Focus first on \n, \t, \\, \" and \'. Also understand raw strings for paths and regular expressions.

items.title: f-Strings
explanation: What are f-Strings?
f-strings, or formatted string literals, provide a simple way to insert variables and expressions directly inside a string.
Definition: An f-string is a string prefixed with f or F where expressions inside {} are evaluated and inserted into the resulting string.
Basic Syntax

name = "John"

message = f"Hello {name}"

print(message)
# Hello John
The f before the opening quote tells Python that the string is an f-string.

Variable
name = "John"
│
▼
f"Hello {name}"
│
▼
"Hello John"
Why Use f-Strings?

Before f-strings, Python programmers commonly used concatenation or formatting methods such as % formatting and str.format(). f-strings are generally easier to read when building strings from variables and expressions.

name = "John"
age = 25

message = f"Name: {name}, Age: {age}"
print(message)
# Name: John, Age: 25
Inserting Multiple Variables

name = "Ravi"
role = "Data Engineer"
city = "Bangalore"

message = f"{name} is a {role} in {city}."

print(message)
# Ravi is a Data Engineer in Bangalore.
Expressions Inside f-Strings
You can place Python expressions inside the curly braces.

a = 10
b = 20

print(f"Total: {a + b}")
# Total: 30

quantity = 5
price = 100

print(f"Total amount: {quantity * price}")
# Total amount: 500
Calling Functions Inside f-Strings
Function calls can also be used inside the expression portion.

name = "python"

print(f"Language: {name.upper()}")
# Language: PYTHON
Using String Methods

name = " john doe "

message = f"Employee: {name.strip().title()}"

print(message)
# Employee: John Doe
Formatting Decimal Numbers
f-strings support format specifications after a colon.

price = 1250.5

print(f"Price: {price:.2f}")
# Price: 1250.50
.2f means display the number as a floating-point value with two digits after the decimal point.
Formatting Percentages

success_rate = 0.956

print(f"Success Rate: {success_rate:.2%}")
# Success Rate: 95.60%
Thousands Separators

records = 1250000

print(f"Records: {records:,}")
# Records: 1,250,000
Data Engineering Use: Number formatting is useful when creating readable reports, logs, monitoring messages, and pipeline summaries.
Formatting Width
You can specify a minimum field width.

name = "John"

print(f"{name:10}")
# John
Alignment

name = "John"

print(f"|{name:<10}|")
print(f"|{name:>10}|")
print(f"|{name:^10}|")

FormatMeaning
<Left aligned
>Right aligned
^Centered
Using Variables in Format Specifications

width = 10
name = "Python"

print(f"|{name:<{width}}|")
Format specifications can themselves contain expressions.
Dates and f-Strings

from datetime import date

today = date.today()

print(f"Today: {today}")
You can also format dates using format specifications.

from datetime import date

today = date.today()

print(f"Date: {today:%Y-%m-%d}")
Debugging with =
Python supports the = form inside f-strings to display both an expression and its value.

records = 1000
status = "SUCCESS"

print(f"{records=}")
print(f"{status=}")

# records=1000
# status='SUCCESS'
Useful Tip: The f"{variable=}" pattern is particularly useful while debugging data-processing code.
Escaping Curly Braces
Curly braces normally indicate an expression in an f-string. To display literal curly braces, use double curly braces.

print(f"{{name}}")
# {name}
This is useful when generating text that itself contains placeholders or JSON-like structures.
f-Strings with Dictionaries
Dictionary values can be inserted using their keys.

employee = {
"name": "John",
"department": "IT"
}

print(f"Employee: {employee['name']}")
print(f"Department: {employee['department']}")
f-Strings with Lists

records = ["R001", "R002", "R003"]

print(f"First record: {records[0]}")
print(f"Total records: {len(records)}")
f-Strings in Data Engineering
f-strings are frequently useful for creating dynamic log messages, file paths, SQL-related text, API URLs, status messages, and pipeline reports.
Example: Pipeline Log

pipeline = "customer_load"
records = 50000
status = "SUCCESS"

log = f"Pipeline={pipeline} | Records={records} | Status={status}"

print(log)
# Pipeline=customer_load | Records=50000 | Status=SUCCESS
Example: Dynamic File Path

year = 2026
month = "09"

path = f"data/{year}/{month}/sales.csv"

print(path)
# data/2026/09/sales.csv
Example: Batch Processing Message

batch_number = 4
total_batches = 10
records = 25000

message = f"Processing batch {batch_number}/{total_batches}: {records:,} records"

print(message)
# Processing batch 4/10: 25,000 records
f-Strings and SQL

f-strings can technically construct SQL text, but inserting untrusted user input directly into SQL this way can create SQL injection vulnerabilities. In production applications, use parameterized queries instead.

table_name = "employees"

query = f"SELECT * FROM {table_name}"
print(query)
# SELECT * FROM employees

Important: Use f-strings for safe dynamic text generation, but do not use them to directly inject untrusted values into SQL queries. Database parameterization should be used for values supplied externally.
f-Strings vs Concatenation

name = "John"
age = 25

# Concatenation
message1 = "Name: " + name + ", Age: " + str(age)

# f-string
message2 = f"Name: {name}, Age: {age}"
The f-string is generally easier to read because values are placed directly where they belong.
f-Strings vs format()

name = "John"
age = 25

# format()
message1 = "Name: {}, Age: {}".format(name, age)

# f-string
message2 = f"Name: {name}, Age: {age}"
Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Forgetting the f before the string.

Mistake 2: Forgetting curly braces around variables.

Mistake 3: Putting quotes incorrectly inside dictionary expressions.

Mistake 4: Confusing {} with literal curly braces.

Mistake 5: Using f-strings to directly insert untrusted values into SQL.

Mistake 6: Performing unnecessarily complex logic inside an f-string instead of calculating the value separately.
Quick Reference

PatternPurpose
f"{name}"Insert a variable
f"{a + b}"Evaluate an expression
f"{value:.2f}"Format decimal value
f"{value:,}"Add thousands separators
f"{value:.2%}"Format percentage
f"{value=}"Debug expression and value
f"{{name}}"Display literal braces
Key Takeaway

Master the basic pattern f"text {expression}". For Data Engineering, f-strings are especially useful for readable logs, dynamic paths, status messages, reports, and controlled dynamic text generation.
practice: Step 1: Create an f-string that displays a person's name and age.

name = "John"
age = 25

message = f"Name: {name}, Age: {age}"
print(message)
Step 2: Insert the result of a calculation directly into an f-string.

quantity = 10
price = 250

print(f"Total: {quantity * price}")
Step 3: Use a string method inside an f-string.

name = " john doe "

print(f"Employee: {name.strip().title()}")
Step 4: Format a decimal value to two decimal places.

amount = 125678.4567

print(f"Amount: {amount:.2f}")
Step 5: Format a large record count using commas.

records = 2500000

print(f"Records processed: {records:,}")
Step 6: Create a pipeline status message.

pipeline = "sales_load"
records = 50000
status = "SUCCESS"

message = f"Pipeline: {pipeline} | Records: {records:,} | Status: {status}"
print(message)
Step 7: Generate a dynamic file path using year and month variables.

year = 2026
month = "09"

path = f"data/{year}/{month}/sales.csv"
print(path)
Step 8: Use the f-string debugging syntax to print both variable names and values.

records = 10000
status = "SUCCESS"

print(f"{records=}")
print(f"{status=}")
Step 9: Create a percentage-formatted pipeline success rate.

success_rate = 0.9875

print(f"Success Rate: {success_rate:.2%}")
Step 10: Work with a dictionary and generate a readable employee message.

employee = {
"id": "EMP101",
"name": "Ravi Kumar",
"department": "Data Engineering"
}

message = f"Employee {employee['id']}: {employee['name']} - {employee['department']}"
print(message)
Step 11: Create a simple batch-processing message.

batch = 3
total_batches = 8
records = 12500

message = f"Processing batch {batch}/{total_batches}: {records:,} records"
print(message)
Step 12: Build a complete pipeline log message using several variables and formatting options.

pipeline = "customer_etl"
batch = 5
records = 125678
duration = 14.56
status = "SUCCESS"

log = f"Pipeline={pipeline} | Batch={batch} | Records={records:,} | Duration={duration:.2f}s | Status={status}"

print(log)

Practice Goal: Be able to use f-strings naturally for variables, expressions, method calls, number formatting, dynamic paths, logs, and pipeline status messages. Understand when f-strings are appropriate and why parameterized queries should be used instead of directly injecting untrusted values into SQL.

qna.q: Q1. What is an f-string?
qna.a: An f-string is a formatted string literal that allows Python expressions to be evaluated inside curly braces.

qna.q: Q2. How do you create an f-string?
qna.a: Prefix the string with f or F, for example: f"Hello {name}".

qna.q: Q3. Where are variables placed in an f-string?
qna.a: Variables and expressions are placed inside curly braces {}.

qna.q: Q4. Can you perform calculations inside an f-string?
qna.a: Yes. Expressions such as {a + b} can be evaluated inside an f-string.

qna.q: Q5. Can you call methods inside an f-string?
qna.a: Yes. For example, f"{name.upper()}" calls upper() and inserts the returned value.

qna.q: Q6. How do you format a floating-point number to two decimal places?
qna.a: Use a format specification such as f"{value:.2f}".

qna.q: Q7. How do you add thousands separators to a number?
qna.a: Use the comma format specifier, such as f"{records:,}".

qna.q: Q8. How do you format a decimal value as a percentage?
qna.a: Use the percentage format, such as f"{rate:.2%}".

qna.q: Q9. What does f"{value=}" do?
qna.a: It displays the expression and its value, which is useful for debugging.

qna.q: Q10. How do you display literal curly braces inside an f-string?
qna.a: Use double curly braces, such as f"{{name}}".

qna.q: Q11. Why are f-strings useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: They make it easy to create readable logs, dynamic file paths, pipeline messages, reports, and other text containing variable values.

qna.q: Q12. Can dictionary values be used inside f-strings?
qna.a: Yes. For example, f"{employee['name']}" can insert a dictionary value.

qna.q: Q13. Can list elements be used inside f-strings?
qna.a: Yes. For example, f"{records[0]}" inserts the first list element.

qna.q: Q14. What is the difference between an f-string and string concatenation?
qna.a: f-strings allow values and expressions to be placed directly inside the string, while concatenation combines strings using operators such as + and may require explicit type conversion.

qna.q: Q15. What happens if you forget the f before the string?
qna.a: The braces are treated as ordinary characters rather than being evaluated as f-string expressions.

qna.q: Q16. Can f-strings contain complex logic?
qna.a: They can contain expressions, but complicated logic is usually clearer when calculated before constructing the final string.

qna.q: Q17. Can f-strings be used to construct SQL?
qna.a: They can construct controlled dynamic SQL text, but untrusted external values should not be directly inserted. Use parameterized queries for SQL values.

qna.q: Q18. Can f-strings be used with dates?
qna.a: Yes. Date objects can be inserted directly or formatted using a date format specification.

qna.q: Q19. What is the main advantage of f-strings?
qna.a: They provide readable and convenient string formatting by allowing expressions directly inside the string.

qna.q: Q20. What is the basic f-string pattern to remember?
qna.a: Remember f"text {expression}".

items.title: Split and Join
explanation: What are split() and join()?
split() and join() are important Python string operations used to move between strings and lists of strings.
Definition: split() breaks one string into multiple pieces and returns a list, while join() combines multiple strings into one string using a separator.

String
"Python,SQL,Pandas"
│
split(",")
↓
["Python", "SQL", "Pandas"]
│
join(" | ")
↓
"Python | SQL | Pandas"
The split() method divides a string into smaller strings and returns them as a list.

text = "Python SQL Pandas"

result = text.split()

print(result)
# ['Python', 'SQL', 'Pandas']
When no separator is supplied, split() separates the string using whitespace.
split() with a Separator
You can specify the delimiter that separates the values.

data = "101,John,Bangalore,50000"

values = data.split(",")

print(values)
# ['101', 'John', 'Bangalore', '50000']
Important: The separator is removed from the resulting pieces. It does not appear as an element in the returned list.
Splitting with a Space

text = "Data Engineering Python"

words = text.split(" ")

print(words)
# ['Data', 'Engineering', 'Python']
For ordinary whitespace-separated text, split() without an argument is generally more robust because it handles runs of whitespace.

text = "Data Engineering Python"

print(text.split())
# ['Data', 'Engineering', 'Python']
split() with maxsplit
The optional maxsplit argument limits how many times Python splits the string.

text = "A-B-C-D-E"

print(text.split("-", 2))
# ['A', 'B', 'C-D-E']
Here, Python performs at most two splits.
Splitting a File Path

path = "data/2026/sales/report.csv"

parts = path.split("/")

print(parts)
# ['data', '2026', 'sales', 'report.csv']
This demonstrates the concept, although Python's pathlib is preferable for reliable filesystem path handling.
Splitting a Simple Data Record

record = "EMP001,John Doe,Data Engineering,50000"

fields = record.split(",")

employee_id = fields[0]
name = fields[1]
department = fields[2]
salary = fields[3]

print(employee_id)
print(name)
print(department)
print(salary)
This is a basic way to understand how delimited text can be separated into fields.
Cleaning Values After split()
Real-world data often contains extra spaces around delimiters. You can clean each value after splitting.

record = "EMP001, John Doe , Bangalore , Completed "

fields = record.split(",")

cleaned = []
for field in fields:
cleaned.append(field.strip())

print(cleaned)
# ['EMP001', 'John Doe', 'Bangalore', 'Completed']
Data Engineering Use: A common preprocessing pattern is split() → clean each field → validate or transform the values → load the structured result.
The join() method combines strings from an iterable into one string.

words = ["Data", "Engineering"]

result = " ".join(words)

print(result)
# Data Engineering
The string before join() becomes the separator.
Different Separators with join()

words = ["Python", "SQL", "Pandas"]

print(",".join(words))
# Python,SQL,Pandas

print(" | ".join(words))
# Python | SQL | Pandas

print("-".join(words))
# Python-SQL-Pandas
join() with an Empty Separator

letters = ["P", "y", "t", "h", "o", "n"]

word = "".join(letters)

print(word)
# Python
Important Rule: join() Expects Strings
The elements being joined must be strings.

numbers = [10, 20, 30]

# This raises TypeError
result = ",".join(numbers)
Convert the values to strings first.

numbers = [10, 20, 30]

result = ",".join(map(str, numbers))

print(result)
# 10,20,30
split() and join() Together
These methods are often used together when transforming text from one delimiter format to another.

data = "Python,SQL,Pandas"

items = data.split(",")
result = " | ".join(items)

print(result)
# Python | SQL | Pandas

Input
"Python,SQL,Pandas"
│
▼
split(",")
│
▼
["Python", "SQL", "Pandas"]
│
▼
join(" | ")
│
▼
"Python | SQL | Pandas"
Changing a Delimiter

data = "EMP001|John|Bangalore|Completed"

fields = data.split("|")
csv_data = ",".join(fields)

print(csv_data)
# EMP001,John,Bangalore,Completed
split() with maxsplit for Key-Value Data
maxsplit is useful when only the first separator has a special meaning.

text = "name=John=Developer"

parts = text.split("=", 1)

print(parts)
# ['name', 'John=Developer']
rsplit()
rsplit() works like split(), but starts splitting from the right.

filename = "sales.2026.final.csv"

print(filename.rsplit(".", 1))
# ['sales.2026.final', 'csv']
This can be useful when you want to separate a final file extension from the rest of a filename.
splitlines()
splitlines() splits a multi-line string into a list of lines.

text = "line one\nline two\nline three"

lines = text.splitlines()

print(lines)
# ['line one', 'line two', 'line three']
Data Engineering Use: splitlines() is useful when processing text content line by line, such as logs or text files.
Partition vs split()
partition() separates a string into exactly three parts: before the separator, the separator itself, and after the separator.

text = "name=John"

print(text.partition("="))
# ('name', '=', 'John')
You do not need to master partition() yet, but knowing it exists is useful.
Common Data Engineering Pattern

raw_data = "101 | John Doe | Bangalore | Completed"

fields = raw_data.split("|")

cleaned_fields = []
for field in fields:
cleaned_fields.append(field.strip())

output = ",".join(cleaned_fields)

print(output)
# 101,John Doe,Bangalore,Completed

Raw Data
│
▼
split()
│
▼
Individual Fields
│
▼
strip() / clean
│
▼
join()
│
▼
Structured Text
split() vs join()

OperationInputOutput
split()StringList of strings
join()Iterable of stringsOne string
Important Methods to Remember

MethodPurpose
split()Split a string into a list
split(separator)Split using a specific delimiter
split(separator, maxsplit)Limit the number of splits
rsplit()Split from the right
splitlines()Split text into lines
join()Combine strings using a separator
partition()Split once into three parts
Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Forgetting that split() returns a list.

Mistake 2: Forgetting that join() requires string elements.

Mistake 3: Writing words.join(",") instead of ",".join(words).

Mistake 4: Using split(",") without considering spaces around commas.

Mistake 5: Manually parsing complex CSV files with split(). Real CSV data can contain quoted delimiters, so use Python's csv module or a suitable data-processing library.
Key Takeaway

Remember the direction: split() converts a string into pieces, while join() combines string pieces into one string. This pattern is fundamental for text processing and later Data Engineering transformations.
practice: Step 1: Split a sentence into individual words.

text = "Python is useful for Data Engineering"

words = text.split()
print(words)
Step 2: Split a comma-separated record into fields.

record = "EMP001,John,Bangalore,Completed"

fields = record.split(",")
print(fields)
Step 3: Convert a list of words into a single sentence using join().

words = ["Data", "Engineering", "is", "interesting"]

sentence = " ".join(words)
print(sentence)
Step 4: Change a pipe-separated record into a comma-separated record.

record = "101|John|Bangalore|50000"

fields = record.split("|")
result = ",".join(fields)

print(result)
Step 5: Clean spaces after splitting a record.

record = "EMP001, John Doe , Bangalore , Completed "

fields = record.split(",")

cleaned = []
for field in fields:
cleaned.append(field.strip())

print(cleaned)
Step 6: Use maxsplit to separate a key from the rest of the value.

data = "message=Data Engineering is interesting"

parts = data.split("=", 1)

print(parts)
Step 7: Use rsplit() to separate a filename from its final extension.

filename = "monthly.sales.report.csv"

parts = filename.rsplit(".", 1)

print(parts)
Step 8: Split a multi-line log into individual lines.

log = "START PROCESSING SUCCESS END"

lines = log.splitlines()
print(lines)
Step 9: Convert a list of numbers into a comma-separated string.

numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

result = ",".join(map(str, numbers))
print(result)
# 10,20,30,40,50
Step 10: Build a complete mini data-cleaning flow: split a raw record, strip every field, convert the status to lowercase, and join the cleaned values using a comma.

raw_record = " EMP001 | JOHN DOE | Bangalore | COMPLETED "

fields = raw_record.split("|")

cleaned = []
for field in fields:
cleaned.append(field.strip())

cleaned[1] = cleaned[1].title()
cleaned[3] = cleaned[3].lower()

result = ",".join(cleaned)
print(result)
# EMP001,John Doe,Bangalore,completed

Practice Goal: Be able to move confidently between raw delimited text and structured lists using split() and join(). Practice cleaning fields between these two operations because this pattern appears frequently in data-processing workflows.

qna.q: Q1. What does split() do?
qna.a: split() divides a string into smaller pieces and returns those pieces as a list.

qna.q: Q2. What does split() return?
qna.a: It returns a list of strings.

qna.q: Q3. What happens when split() is called without an argument?
qna.a: It splits the string around whitespace and returns the resulting words or groups of non-whitespace characters.

qna.q: Q4. How do you split a comma-separated string?
qna.a: Use string.split(",").

qna.q: Q5. What is maxsplit?
qna.a: maxsplit limits the maximum number of splits performed by split().

qna.q: Q6. What does join() do?
qna.a: join() combines strings from an iterable into one string using the calling string as the separator.

qna.q: Q7. What is the correct syntax for joining a list?
qna.a: Use separator.join(list), for example: ",".join(items).

qna.q: Q8. Why does numbers = [10, 20, 30]; ",".join(numbers) fail?
qna.a: join() expects its elements to be strings, but the list contains integers.

qna.q: Q9. How can you join a list of numbers?
qna.a: Convert the numbers to strings first, for example: ",".join(map(str, numbers)).

qna.q: Q10. What is the difference between split() and join()?
qna.a: split() generally converts one string into a list of strings, while join() combines an iterable of strings into one string.

qna.q: Q11. Can split() and join() be used together?
qna.a: Yes. A common pattern is to split raw text, clean or transform the resulting fields, and then join them using another separator.

qna.q: Q12. What does rsplit() do?
qna.a: rsplit() behaves like split() but performs splitting from the right side.

qna.q: Q13. What does splitlines() do?
qna.a: It splits a multi-line string into a list of individual lines.

qna.q: Q14. How can you remove spaces from fields after split()?
qna.a: Call strip() on each resulting field, for example by looping through the list.

qna.q: Q15. What is the output of "A-B-C".split("-")?
qna.a: It returns ['A', 'B', 'C'].

qna.q: Q16. What is the output of "A-B-C".split("-", 1)?
qna.a: It returns ['A', 'B-C'] because only one split is performed.

qna.q: Q17. What is the difference between split() and partition()?
qna.a: split() can produce multiple pieces and returns a list, while partition() splits once and returns a three-element tuple containing the part before the separator, the separator, and the part after it.

qna.q: Q18. Why is split() useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It can separate delimited text into fields so the values can be cleaned, validated, transformed, or loaded into structured data.

qna.q: Q19. Should split() always be used to parse CSV files?
qna.a: No. Real CSV data can contain quoted fields and delimiters inside values, so Python's csv module or an appropriate data-processing library should be used.

qna.q: Q20. What is the most important pattern to remember?
qna.a: Remember: string.split(separator) turns text into a list, and separator.join(strings) turns strings back into one text value.

items.title: `open()`
explanation: What is open()?
The built-in open() function is used to open a file so that Python can read from it, write to it, append data to it, or perform other file operations.
Definition: open() creates and returns a file object connected to a file. You can then use methods such as read(), write(), and close() to work with that file.
Basic Syntax
file = open("filename.txt", "r")

ArgumentPurpose
filenameName or path of the file
modeSpecifies how the file should be opened
Basic Example

file = open("data.txt", "r")

content = file.read()
print(content)

file.close()
Here, Python opens data.txt in read mode, reads its content, prints it, and then closes the file.

File on Disk
│
▼
open()
│
▼
File Object
│
├── read()
├── write()
└── close()
File Path
The first argument can be a relative path or an absolute path.

# Relative path
file = open("data.txt", "r")

# File inside a folder
file = open("data/input.txt", "r")
A relative path is interpreted relative to the program's current working directory.
Opening an Absolute Path
file = open("C:\\Users\\John\\data\\input.txt", "r")
On Windows, remember that backslashes can introduce escape sequences. A raw string can make paths easier to write.
file = open(r"C:\Users\John\data\input.txt", "r")
File Modes
The second argument specifies the mode in which the file is opened.

ModeMeaning
rRead
wWrite
aAppend
xCreate a new file
r+Read and write
w+Write and read
a+Append and read
Default Mode
If no mode is supplied, open() uses read mode by default.
file = open("data.txt")
This is equivalent to:
file = open("data.txt", "r")
Opening a File in Read Mode

file = open("data.txt", "r")

content = file.read()
print(content)

file.close()
Read mode is used when you only need to retrieve existing file content.
Opening a File in Write Mode

file = open("output.txt", "w")

file.write("Hello Python")

file.close()
Warning: Opening an existing file with w can overwrite its existing content. Use this mode carefully.
Opening a File in Append Mode

file = open("log.txt", "a")

file.write("New log entry\n")

file.close()
Append mode adds new content to the end of the file without replacing the existing content.
Opening a File in Create Mode

file = open("new_file.txt", "x")

file.write("New file")
file.close()
Mode x creates a new file and raises FileExistsError if the file already exists.
open() Returns a File Object

file = open("data.txt", "r")

print(type(file))
# <class '_io.TextIOWrapper'>

file.close()
The returned object provides methods and properties for interacting with the opened file.
Checking Whether a File Is Closed

file = open("data.txt", "r")

print(file.closed)
# False

file.close()

print(file.closed)
# True
Why close() Is Important
An opened file uses system resources. Closing the file releases those resources and ensures pending writes are properly completed.
Important: Although you can manually call close(), the recommended approach is to use with open(...). The with statement automatically closes the file.
open() with with

with open("data.txt", "r") as file:
content = file.read()
print(content)
After the with block finishes, the file is automatically closed.

with open()
│
▼
Open File
│
▼
Read / Write
│
▼
Exit Block
│
▼
Automatically Closed
Encoding
You can specify the character encoding when opening a text file.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
content = file.read()
print(content)
Specifying the encoding explicitly is a good practice when working with text data, especially across different systems.
Text Mode and Binary Mode
By default, open() works with text files. Binary mode uses b.

# Text mode
file = open("data.txt", "r")

# Binary mode
file = open("image.jpg", "rb")

ModePurpose
rRead text
rbRead binary data
wWrite text
wbWrite binary data
For this Python foundation section, focus primarily on text files. Binary file processing can be learned when needed.
Opening a Non-Existing File in Read Mode
file = open("missing.txt", "r")
If the file does not exist, Python raises FileNotFoundError.
Opening a File with a Relative Directory

with open("data/input/customers.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
content = file.read()
The directories in the path must exist. open() does not automatically create missing parent directories.
Basic Data Engineering Example
Data Engineers frequently receive raw text files that need to be read before cleaning and transformation.

with open("customers.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
raw_data = file.read()

print(raw_data)

Raw File
│
▼
open()
│
▼
File Object
│
▼
read()
│
▼
Raw Text
│
▼
Cleaning / Transformation
│
▼
Structured Data
Reading a File Line by Line
A file object can be iterated over directly, which allows processing one line at a time.

with open("customers.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
for line in file:
print(line.strip())
Data Engineering Connection: Processing a file line by line can avoid loading the entire file into memory at once. This becomes important when working with large files.
Writing Pipeline Output

records_processed = 1000

with open("pipeline.log", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
file.write(f"Records processed: {records_processed}\n")
This demonstrates how file handling can be used for simple pipeline output or logs. Production logging is covered separately in the roadmap.
Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Forgetting to close a manually opened file.

Mistake 2: Using w when you intended to append, which can overwrite existing content.

Mistake 3: Reading a file that does not exist and not handling FileNotFoundError.

Mistake 4: Forgetting to specify an appropriate encoding for text data.

Mistake 5: Using string operations to handle complex CSV data instead of a CSV parser or appropriate data-processing library.

Mistake 6: Loading a very large file completely into memory without considering a line-by-line or chunked approach.
Quick Reference

CodePurpose
open("file.txt", "r")Open for reading
open("file.txt", "w")Open for writing
open("file.txt", "a")Open for appending
open("file.txt", "x")Create a new file
open("file.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8")Open text file with explicit encoding
open("file.txt", "rb")Open binary file for reading
with open(...) as file:Open and automatically close the file
Key Takeaway

open() connects Python to a file and returns a file object. Learn the basic modes r, w, and a, understand the danger of w, specify encoding for text files when appropriate, and prefer with open() so files are closed automatically.
practice: Step 1: Create a text file named data.txt manually and open it in read mode.

file = open("data.txt", "r")

print(file)

file.close()
Step 2: Read the complete contents of a text file using open() and read().

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
content = file.read()

print(content)
Step 3: Create a new output file using write mode and store a simple message.

with open("output.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
file.write("Data Engineering")
Step 4: Append another line without replacing the existing content.

with open("output.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as file:
file.write("\nPython File Handling")
Step 5: Read the file line by line.

with open("output.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
for line in file:
print(line.strip())
Step 6: Check the closed property before and after manually closing a file.

file = open("data.txt", "r")

print(file.closed)

file.close()

print(file.closed)
Step 7: Create a small raw-data file and read its contents into a variable.

with open("customers.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
file.write("C001,John,Bangalore ")
file.write("C002,Ravi,Hyderabad ")
file.write("C003,Anu,Chennai ")

with open("customers.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
raw_data = file.read()

print(raw_data)
Step 8: Read the same file line by line and remove the newline character from each line.

with open("customers.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
for line in file:
print(line.strip())
Step 9: Try opening a file that does not exist and observe the FileNotFoundError.

with open("missing_file.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
content = file.read()
Step 10: Build a simple file-based data-processing flow: read raw records, process each line, and write the result to another file.

with open("customers.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as source:
with open("cleaned_customers.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as target:
for line in source:
cleaned_line = line.strip().lower()
target.write(cleaned_line + "\n")

Practice Goal: Understand how open() connects Python to files, know the purpose of the basic file modes, use with open() correctly, and be able to read and write simple text data. Do not go deeply into CSV, JSON, Parquet, or Avro here; those have dedicated topics later in the roadmap.

qna.q: Q1. What is open() in Python?
qna.a: open() is a built-in function used to open a file and return a file object.

qna.q: Q2. What does open("data.txt", "r") do?
qna.a: It opens data.txt in read mode.

qna.q: Q3. What is the default mode of open()?
qna.a: The default mode is r, which means read mode.

qna.q: Q4. What does r mean?
qna.a: r opens a file for reading.

qna.q: Q5. What does w mean?
qna.a: w opens a file for writing. If the file already exists, its existing content can be overwritten.

qna.q: Q6. What does a mean?
qna.a: a opens a file for appending, so new content is written at the end.

qna.q: Q7. What does x mean?
qna.a: x creates a new file and raises FileExistsError if the file already exists.

qna.q: Q8. What does open() return?
qna.a: It returns a file object that provides methods and properties for interacting with the file.

qna.q: Q9. Why should a file be closed?
qna.a: Closing releases system resources and ensures pending writes are properly completed.

qna.q: Q10. What is the recommended way to open a file?
qna.a: Use a with statement, such as with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:, because the file is automatically closed when the block finishes.

qna.q: Q11. What does encoding="utf-8" do?
qna.a: It specifies the character encoding used to decode text when reading or encode text when writing.

qna.q: Q12. What happens if you try to open a missing file in r mode?
qna.a: Python raises FileNotFoundError.

qna.q: Q13. What happens if you open an existing file using w mode?
qna.a: The file is opened for writing and its existing content is truncated, so previous content can be lost.

qna.q: Q14. What is the difference between w and a?
qna.a: w writes from the beginning and truncates an existing file, while a preserves existing content and appends new content at the end.

qna.q: Q15. What is the difference between text mode and binary mode?
qna.a: Text mode works with text strings and encoding, while binary mode works with bytes and uses modes such as rb and wb.

qna.q: Q16. Can open() create a missing directory?
qna.a: No. open() can create a file in an existing directory, but it does not automatically create missing parent directories.

qna.q: Q17. Why is with open() useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It safely manages file resources while reading or writing raw data and ensures the file is closed automatically.

qna.q: Q18. Can a large file be processed without reading the entire file into memory?
qna.a: Yes. A file can be iterated line by line, allowing records to be processed incrementally.

qna.q: Q19. Should complex CSV files be processed using only open() and split()?
qna.a: No. open() provides file access, but real CSV parsing should use Python's csv module or an appropriate data-processing library.

qna.q: Q20. What are the most important things to remember about open()?
qna.a: Know the basic modes r, w, and a; understand that w can overwrite existing data; specify encoding for text when appropriate; and prefer with open() for automatic resource management.

items.title: File Modes
explanation: What are File Modes?
When using Python's open() function, the file mode tells Python what you intend to do with the file, such as read, write, append, or create it.
Definition: A file mode is a string passed to open() that determines how Python opens and interacts with a file.
Basic Syntax
open("filename.txt", "mode")

open("data.txt", "r")
│ │
│ └── File Mode
│
└──────── File Name
Main File Modes

ModePurposeFile Must Exist?Existing Content
rReadYesPreserved
wWriteNoOverwritten if file exists
aAppendNoPreserved
xCreate new fileNoFails if file exists
1. Read Mode — r
r opens an existing file for reading.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
content = file.read()
print(content)
If the file does not exist, Python raises FileNotFoundError.
Important: Read mode does not allow you to write new content to the file.
2. Write Mode — w
w opens a file for writing.

with open("output.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
file.write("Hello Python")
If the file does not exist, Python creates it.
If the file already exists, its existing content is truncated before writing.

Existing File
"Old Data"
│
▼
open(..., "w")
│
▼
Existing content removed
│
▼
New content written
Warning: w can destroy existing file content. Never use it when you intend to preserve the existing data.
3. Append Mode — a
a opens a file for adding new content at the end.

with open("log.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as file:
file.write("New log entry\n")
If the file does not exist, Python creates it.
If the file already exists, its existing content is preserved and new data is added at the end.

Existing File
"Old Data"
│
▼
open(..., "a")
│
▼
Existing content preserved
│
▼
New data added at end
w vs a

# w → replaces existing content
with open("data.txt", "w") as file:
file.write("New Data")

# a → keeps existing content and adds to the end
with open("data.txt", "a") as file:
file.write("More Data")

ModeIf file existsIf file does not exist
wExisting content is truncatedNew file is created
aContent is preserved and new data is appendedNew file is created
4. Exclusive Creation Mode — x
x creates a new file only if it does not already exist.

with open("new_file.txt", "x", encoding="utf-8") as file:
file.write("First content")
If the file already exists, Python raises FileExistsError.
Use Case: x is useful when you want Python to fail rather than accidentally overwrite an existing file.
5. Read and Write Mode — r+
r+ opens an existing file for both reading and writing.

with open("data.txt", "r+", encoding="utf-8") as file:
content = file.read()
print(content)

file.write("New data")
The file must already exist. The existing content is not automatically truncated when the file is opened.
6. Write and Read Mode — w+
w+ allows both writing and reading, but opening the file truncates its existing content.

with open("data.txt", "w+", encoding="utf-8") as file:
file.write("Hello")
file.seek(0)
print(file.read())
Important: Because w+ truncates an existing file, use it carefully.
7. Append and Read Mode — a+
a+ allows both appending and reading.

with open("log.txt", "a+", encoding="utf-8") as file:
file.write("New entry\n")
file.seek(0)
print(file.read())
New data is written at the end, while reading is also allowed.
Text Mode — t
t represents text mode. It is the default mode when working with text files.
open("data.txt", "rt")
This is equivalent to:
open("data.txt", "r")
Binary Mode — b
b opens a file in binary mode. Binary mode works with bytes rather than normal text strings.

with open("image.jpg", "rb") as file:
data = file.read()
Common combinations include rb for binary reading and wb for binary writing.

ModeMeaning
rtRead text
rbRead binary
wtWrite text
wbWrite binary
atAppend text
abAppend binary
File Mode Combination Structure

Basic mode
│
├── r → read
├── w → write
├── a → append
└── x → create

Optional modifier
│
├── + → read and write
├── b → binary
└── t → text
Examples of Mode Combinations

ModeMeaning
rRead text
rbRead binary
r+Read and write text
rb+Read and write binary
wWrite text, truncating existing file
wbWrite binary, truncating existing file
w+Write and read text, truncating existing file
aAppend text
abAppend binary
a+Append and read text
File Position and seek()
When reading and writing files, Python maintains a current file position. seek() can move that position.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
print(file.read(5))
file.seek(0)
print(file.read())
File positioning is useful with modes that support both reading and writing, although it is not necessary to master advanced file positioning at this stage.
Encoding with File Modes
For text files, you can specify the encoding together with the mode.

with open("customers.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
data = file.read()
For binary modes such as rb and wb, you work with bytes rather than text encoding through open().
Data Engineering Examples
Different file modes correspond to different stages of a simple data workflow.

# Read raw source data
with open("source.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
raw_data = file.read()

# Write a fresh transformed output
with open("cleaned.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
file.write(raw_data)

# Append a processing note
with open("pipeline.log", "a", encoding="utf-8") as file:
file.write("Pipeline completed\n")

Source File
│
│ r
▼
Read Data
│
▼
Transform
│
│ w
▼
Output File

Pipeline Events
│
│ a
▼
Log File
Choosing the Correct Mode

RequirementMode
Only read an existing filer
Create or completely replace outputw
Add data to existing filea
Create only if file does not existx
Read and write existing filer+
Read and write while replacing existing contentw+
Read and appenda+
Work with binary dataAdd b
Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Using w when you intended to preserve existing data.

Mistake 2: Using a when you need to replace the existing file.

Mistake 3: Assuming x silently opens an existing file. It raises FileExistsError instead.

Mistake 4: Trying to read from a file opened only with w.

Mistake 5: Forgetting that r requires the file to already exist.

Mistake 6: Treating binary data as ordinary text.

Mistake 7: Forgetting that w+ truncates an existing file.
Quick Memory Trick

r → Read
w → Write / Replace
a → Add
x → Create only
+ → Read + Write
b → Binary
t → Text
Key Takeaway
For the Python foundation, master r, w, a, and x first. Then understand + for combined reading/writing and b for binary files. The most important safety rule is: w can overwrite existing content.
practice: Step 1: Open an existing text file in read mode and print its contents.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
print(file.read())
Step 2: Open a file in write mode and create fresh content.

with open("output.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
file.write("First version")
Step 3: Run the write operation again with different content and observe what happens to the previous content.

with open("output.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
file.write("Second version")
Step 4: Use append mode to add a new line while preserving existing content.

with open("output.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as file:
file.write("\nThird version")
Step 5: Use exclusive creation mode to create a new file and observe what happens if you run it again.

with open("new_file.txt", "x", encoding="utf-8") as file:
file.write("Created once")
Step 6: Create a simple pipeline log using append mode.

with open("pipeline.log", "a", encoding="utf-8") as log:
log.write("Pipeline started\n")
log.write("Pipeline completed\n")
Step 7: Practice the difference between w and a using a small data file.

# Replace existing content
with open("records.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
file.write("R001\n")

# Preserve existing content and add another record
with open("records.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as file:
file.write("R002\n")
Step 8: Use r+ to open an existing file for both reading and writing.

with open("data.txt", "r+", encoding="utf-8") as file:
content = file.read()
print(content)
file.write("\nNew content")
Step 9: Create a binary file and read it using binary mode.

with open("sample.bin", "wb") as file:
file.write(b"ABC")

with open("sample.bin", "rb") as file:
data = file.read()
print(data)
Step 10: Given a data pipeline requirement, select the correct mode: read source data, replace a generated output, append logs, and create a file only if it does not exist.

# Read source → r
# Replace generated output → w
# Add pipeline log → a
# Create only if missing → x

Practice Goal: Be able to select the correct file mode based on the required operation. You should clearly understand the difference between r, w, a, and x, especially the risk of overwriting data with w.

qna.q: Q1. What is a file mode?
qna.a: A file mode tells Python how a file should be opened and what operations are allowed.

qna.q: Q2. What does r mean?
qna.a: r opens a file for reading. The file must already exist.

qna.q: Q3. What does w mean?
qna.a: w opens a file for writing. It creates the file if necessary and truncates an existing file.

qna.q: Q4. What does a mean?
qna.a: a opens a file for appending. Existing content is preserved and new content is added at the end.

qna.q: Q5. What does x mean?
qna.a: x creates a new file and raises FileExistsError if the file already exists.

qna.q: Q6. What is the biggest risk of w mode?
qna.a: Opening an existing file with w truncates its existing content, which can cause data loss.

qna.q: Q7. What happens if r mode is used for a missing file?
qna.a: Python raises FileNotFoundError.

qna.q: Q8. What happens if a mode is omitted?
qna.a: open() defaults to r mode.

qna.q: Q9. What is r+?
qna.a: r+ opens an existing file for both reading and writing without automatically truncating it.

qna.q: Q10. What is w+?
qna.a: w+ opens a file for reading and writing, but truncates an existing file when it is opened.

qna.q: Q11. What is a+?
qna.a: a+ opens a file for both reading and appending. New writes are made at the end of the file.

qna.q: Q12. What does b mean in a file mode?
qna.a: b means binary mode, which works with bytes rather than text strings.

qna.q: Q13. What does t mean in a file mode?
qna.a: t means text mode, which is the default mode for ordinary text files.

qna.q: Q14. What does rb mean?
qna.a: rb opens a file for reading binary data.

qna.q: Q15. What does wb mean?
qna.a: wb opens a file for writing binary data and truncates an existing file.

qna.q: Q16. Which mode should you use to add a new log entry without deleting previous entries?
qna.a: Use append mode, a.

qna.q: Q17. Which mode should you use when you want to create a file only if it does not already exist?
qna.a: Use x mode.

qna.q: Q18. Which mode is commonly used to read raw source data in a Data Engineering pipeline?
qna.a: r mode is commonly used to read an existing text source file.

qna.q: Q19. Which mode is useful for writing a fresh generated output file?
qna.a: w mode is useful when the intention is to create or completely replace the output.

qna.q: Q20. What is the easiest way to remember the main modes?
qna.a: r = read, w = write/replace, a = append/add, x = create only, + = read and write, b = binary, and t = text.

items.title: with open()
explanation: What is with open()?
with open() is the preferred way to open and work with files in Python. It automatically closes the file after the indented block finishes, even if an error occurs.

with open("data.txt", "r") as file:
    data = file.read()
    print(data)
Definition: The with statement manages the file resource automatically. When the block ends, Python closes the file for you.
Why use with open()?
When a file is opened, Python creates a file object that uses an operating-system resource. The file should be closed after use.

Python Program
      |
      v
with open("data.txt")
      |
      v
  File is opened
      |
      v
  Read / Write data
      |
      v
  Block finishes
      |
      v
  File automatically closed
Without with, you normally need to close the file manually:

file = open("data.txt", "r")
try:
    data = file.read()
    print(data)
finally:
    file.close()
With with, the same resource-management logic becomes much simpler:

with open("data.txt", "r") as file:
    data = file.read()
    print(data)
Basic Syntax

with open("file_path", "mode") as file:
    # file operations
The main parts are:

PartMeaning
withStarts a managed resource block.
open()Opens the file and returns a file object.
File pathSpecifies which file to open.
ModeSpecifies how the file will be opened.
as fileStores the file object in the variable file.
Reading a File
The most common read operation is using "r" mode.

with open("employees.txt", "r") as file:
    data = file.read()

print(data)
Notice that print(data) is outside the with block. The data has already been stored in the variable.
Reading Line by Line
For large files, reading the entire file using read() may consume a lot of memory. A file object can be iterated line by line.

with open("large_data.txt", "r") as file:
    for line in file:
        print(line.strip())
Data Engineering Tip: For large text files, processing one line at a time is often more memory-efficient than loading the complete file into memory.
Writing to a File
You can also use with open() for writing.

with open("output.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("Data Engineering\n")
    file.write("Python\n")
When the with block finishes, Python automatically closes the file.
Appending Data
Use "a" mode when you want to add data to the end of an existing file.

with open("pipeline.log", "a") as file:
    file.write("Pipeline completed\n")
This is useful for simple log files where new information needs to be added without removing existing content.
Using Encoding
When working with text files, it is good practice to explicitly specify the encoding when you know the expected encoding.

with open("employees.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()

print(data)
encoding="utf-8" helps Python correctly interpret Unicode text.
File Automatically Closes

with open("data.txt", "r") as file:
    data = file.read()
    print(file.closed)   # False

print(file.closed)       # True
Inside the block, the file is open. After leaving the block, Python closes it automatically.
What Happens if an Error Occurs?
One major advantage of with open() is that the file is still properly closed if an exception occurs inside the block.

try:
    with open("data.txt", "r") as file:
        data = file.read()
        result = 10 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("An error occurred")
The exception does not prevent the context manager from performing the file cleanup.
Relative and Absolute Paths
with open() accepts both relative and absolute file paths.

# Relative path
with open("data/input.txt", "r") as file:
    data = file.read()

# Windows absolute path
with open(r"C:\data\input.txt", "r") as file:
    data = file.read()
Raw strings such as r"C:\data\input.txt" are useful for Windows paths because backslashes are otherwise interpreted as escape sequences.
Using pathlib with with open()
For more reliable path handling, Python provides pathlib.

from pathlib import Path

file_path = Path("data") / "employees.txt"

with open(file_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()

print(data)
Data Engineering Connection: Data pipelines commonly work with files located in different folders. pathlib makes path construction clearer and more portable.
Reading a Large File
A common Data Engineering pattern is processing a large text file incrementally.

with open("transactions.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for line in file:
        line = line.strip()
        if line:
            print(line)

Large File
    |
    v
open with with
    |
    v
read one line
    |
    v
process line
    |
    v
read next line
    |
    v
file ends
    |
    v
file automatically closed
Important Difference: read() vs Iterating

ApproachBehaviorTypical Use
read()Reads the complete remaining content.Small text files.
readline()Reads one line.Controlled line-by-line reading.
readlines()Reads lines into a list.When a list of lines is specifically needed.
for line in fileIterates through the file line by line.Large files and streaming-style processing.
Common Mistakes

• Forgetting the indentation after with.
  • Using "w" when you actually wanted to append data.
  • Trying to read a file that does not exist in "r" mode.
  • Ignoring encoding problems when processing text from different systems.
  • Loading very large files completely into memory without considering line-by-line processing.
  • Trying to use the file object for normal I/O after the with block has ended.
Data Engineering Example
Suppose a pipeline receives a daily application log file. A simple Python process can read the file and identify error records.

with open("application.log", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for line in file:
        if "ERROR" in line:
            print(line.strip())

application.log
      |
      v
with open()
      |
      v
Read line by line
      |
      v
Check for ERROR
      |
      v
Process matching records
This is only a basic example. Later in the roadmap, dedicated topics such as logging, CSV/JSON, ETL, data quality, and data pipelines will cover more appropriate production techniques.
Quick Summary

ConceptKey Point
with open()Preferred pattern for working with files.
as fileStores the file object in a variable.
Automatic closingThe file is closed when the block ends.
Error safetyCleanup occurs even when an exception happens.
Large filesIterate line by line when appropriate.
encoding="utf-8"Explicitly specifies text encoding.
practice: Step 1: Create a file named data.txt and write three lines of text into it manually.

Python
SQL
Data Engineering
Step 2: Read the complete file using with open() and print its contents.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()

print(data)
Step 3: Read the same file line by line.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for line in file:

Step 4: Create a new file called pipeline.log and write two messages into it.

with open("pipeline.log", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("Pipeline started\n")
    file.write("Pipeline completed\n")
Step 5: Append another message without deleting the existing content.

with open("pipeline.log", "a", encoding="utf-8") as file:

Step 6: Create a large text file and process it line by line. Count how many lines contain the word ERROR.

Step 7: Use pathlib to construct the file path instead of manually joining folder names.

file_path = Path("data") / "input.txt"

with open(file_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
